LABOUR. All life is labour, only dm* is rest: Nature again prepares her flow'r and leaf When sun-browned autumn reels with fruit and sheaf. And woods are in their golden vesture drest ; The mountain drains the torrent from the breast Of clouds full pastured where the tropic reef oce,an-foamed, and pours along its fief Of purple plain, wide flowing rivers prest With clover banks and slopes of waving corn; Th' unwearied sun keeps evermore his round Among the siren stars, as on the morn He first rose up amid the blue profound, Of God's almighty will and labour born. While angels gazed and sang in heaven's bound. ir-C'assell's Family Magazine.

LITTLE FEET. Two little feet so small that both may nestle In one caressing hand Two tender feet upon the untried border Of life's mysterious land. Dimpled and soft, and pink as peach tree blossoms In April's fragrant days; How can they walk among the briery tangles Edging the world's rough ways? These white-rose feet along the doubtful future Must bear a woman's load. Alas: since woman has the heaviest burden, And walks the hardest road. Love for awhile will make the path before them All dainty, smooth, and fair— Will cull away the bramb s,lettingonly The roses blossom there. But when the mother's watchful eyes are shrouded gaheet loeff tm en, them then? without her guiding, AnAldvwty thesesfhall r dioW rect ti blindly in the darkness Will they go stumbling Of sorrow's tearful shades, Or find the upland slopes of Peace and Beauty Whose sunlight never fades 2 Will they go toiling up Ambition's summit. The common world above. Or, in some nameless vale, securely sheltered, Walk side by side with Love? Some feet there be which walk Life's track unwounded, Which find lint pleasant ways ; Some hearts there be to which this life is only A round of happy days. But they are few. Far more there are who wander Without a hope or friend; Who find their journey full of pains and losses, And long to reach the end. HOW shall it be with her, the tender stranger, Fair-faced and gentle-eyed; Before whose unstained feet the world's rude highway Stretches so strange and wide? Ah who may read the future? For our darling We crave all blessings sweet, And pray that He who feeds the crying ravens Will guide the baby's feet.

- - - A Stirring Time: Making porridge. A paper mill—a quarrel between two editors. The giving that costa is the giving that counts. A man's character is like a fence—it cannot be streng- thened by whitewash. No man can do the best work that is in him without a cer- tain amount of kindly sympathy. A NEW Lastrar.— A London tradesman advertises "Ladies shawls for dinner and breakfast." What glorious object does a boy getting up in the morn- ing resemble? The rising sun, of course. . A manufacturing wire-weerker in an advertisement invites the public to come and see hie invisible wire fences. "Your handwriting is very bad." " Yes ; but don't you see, if I were to write better people would find out how I spell?" "Tommy," said a mother to her seven-year-old-boy, "you must not interrupt me when I am talking with ladies. You must wait till we stop, and then you can talk." "Bat you never stop," retorted the boy. Little Freddy was having his hair combed by his mother, and he grumbled at the operation. " Why, Freddy, you oughtn't to make such a fuss. I don't when my hair is combed." "Yes, bat your hair ain't hitched to your head." • Volunteer Captain (Acting Major first time): "Now then, what are you boys staring at? Did you never see a war- horse before?" Boys (who had followed, expecting a "Aye—we've whiles seen a waur horse, but never a wanr rider !"—Punch. Until churches are furnished with mirrore, women will continue to keep their bonnets on during the service. With- out a looking-glase, a bonnet once taken off could never be pat on again. Thatls to say, we never saw or heard of such a thing.—Boston Transcript. Infinite toil would not enable you to. sweep away a mist, I 'out by ascending a little you may often look over it alto- gether. So it is with our moral improvement. We wrestle fiercely with a vicious habit, which could have no hold upon us if we ascended into a higher atmosphere.—Helpe. Tarn your calmer eyes To the fair page of knowledge. It is power I give; and power is precious. It is strength To live fonr-equare, careless of outward shows And self-sufficing. It is clearer right To know the rule of life, the Eternal scheme; And, knowing it, to do and not to err, And, doing, to be blest. WANM MILE as e. SEVERAGE.—MiIk heated to much above 100 degrees Fahrenheit loses for the time a degree of its sweetness and its density. No One who, fatigued by over-exertion of body or mind, has ever experienced the reviving influence of a tumbler of this beverage, heated as hot as it can be sipped, will willingly forego a resort to it because of its having been rendered somewhat less accep- table to the palate. The promptness with which its cordial itfluence is felt is indeed surprising. Some portion of it seems to be digested and appropriated almost onmeditlifflY • and many who fancy that they need alcoholic stimulants when exhausted 1,-• -- I." - -4 wen and In the simple draught iterNealerit. that will be abundantly satisfying and Tee:: enduring in its effects. HotrE FRIENDSRIPS.—If we cultivate home friendships with the same assiduity that we give to those outside, they will yield us even richer and fairer returns. There is no • friendship so pare and beautiful in its nature, so rich and fall in its power of blessing, or so singularly rare in its on- currenze, as that between parents and their grown-up sons and daughters. Where the parental and filial instincts are supplemented by that higher and mere spiritual affection that binds together minds in intellectual communion and souls in heartfelt sympathy, few deeper or more delightful fr:einlshiPs can be imagined. The guardian and dependant gradually lose themselves in the dear companion and true friend of later life; and youth becomes wiser and age brighter, and both nobler and happier in this loving and abiding union. IGNORANT Fout.—SCOn after the arrival of the welcome news from Waterloo, a Cornish spire, meeting some miners, thought to gratify their ears by the announcement that peace had come at last, but was dumbfoundered by one of them replying, "I never heard as there'd been war yet!" Such indifference regarding what is going on in the world is nothing uncommon. Codrington, a few days after his re- turn home as victor of Navarino, was greeted by a country aceuaintance with, "How are you Codrington I haven't seen you for some time. Had any shooting lately ?" "Yes, I have had some remarkable shooting," said the admiral as he passed on his way. At the anxious time when war or peace depended upon America's answer to England's demand for the release of Messrs. Mason and Slidell, a gentleman going into the smoking•room of a Welsh hotel was astonished to find the company there, not only unaware of the existence of the envoys of the south, but actually ignorant that there was any trouble at all in the States—an ignorance shared by the farmer who declined to subscribe to the Lancashire Relief Fund on the plea that Lancashire folk bad no business to go to war with the Yankees. M. Thiers one day entered a cottage near Canterets, occupied by an old roan named Perelas, and enquired if he was not at the school of the Trois Frerer with Thiers. " Thiers! Thiers !" echoed the cakeseller ; "yes, I remember him, a very mischievous boy." " Well," said the great little man, lam he." The statesman's old schoolmate, not at all disturbed, asked what he was doing. " Well," said the president, " I'm doing nothing just now, but for alum; time I was minister." What sort of a minister the village Nestor supposed he had been was shown by his replying, " Ah, you were a Pro- testant, weren't you ?" It would be interesting to know how many of the electors of the United Kingdom have any Idea of what they mean when they dub themselves Liberal or Conservative. A vast number, we fancy, are no better informed than Stephen Noyes, the Stroud Voter, who de- posed that he only knew of two parties, the yellows and the blues; and, being a man who could not understand, was unable to say whether Mr. Disraeli was a yellow or a blue— inaeed, he had never heard that gentleman's name before. That of Mr. Gladstone was more familiar to him ; he was a Liberal, he supposed. Pressed to give his notion of what Liberals were, he replied, " I think they be the best side of the Party," under which impression he had doubtless cast his vote. Such political innocence is far more common than some people imagine. We once interviewed an old voter in the Midlands, who protested he was neither Liberal or Tory, blue or yellow; he was a cocked hat, like his father and grandfather before him ; but what a cocked hat might be, as to principles, was more than he or anyone else could tell us. He had seen a good many tough contests in his time, and with all his ignorance of political parties was not so verdant as the three young fellows who once stood gazing at a placard at Wymondham, informing passers by that the Norwich election had resulted thus :

You see, when it freezes at Cairo, it must be pretty cold; so they say so many degrees below Cairo." The unconvinced one replied: "No, they don't, you've got the wrong word, it's so many degrees below Nero. RENEGE POR A HARD MILKER.—J. EL O. E., Pike County, Penn. :—A hard milking cow may be managed as follows: Make of some whalebone or ivory a long thin plug for each teat, larger in the middle to prevent it from slip- ping out, and with a head of sufficient size to prevent it from slipping in. Make the plugs very smooth, and, after greasing them with glycerine and sweet-oil mixed, insert them in the teats and keep them in the ducts except when milking. In a short time the passage will be permanently enlarged.—New York Tribune. FAILURES AMONG FARMERS IN GREAT BRITAIN AND IRELAND.—The editor of Kemp's-Mercantile Gazette has pre- pared for Land a statistical abstract of failures among farmers from January 1, 1867, to November 2, 1881. The document shows that where the total number of failures of farmers in the United Kingdom in 1867 was 328, it was 1,405 in 1879, and 1,254 in 1880. The figures for 1879 were almost double those of the previous year. So far this year the number has dwindled down to 826, but there are two months yet to be added to that calculation. Ireland, how- ever, has until the last nine years enjoyed an almost total Immunity from agricultural failures, for during the six years 1867-72 there were only 13 failures among farmers— a fraction over two per annum. Since then, however; the tale hasteen somewhat more sorrowful, the 25 failures of 1873 gradually increasing until they reached 99 in 1879. At that point things began to mend, and in 1880 the failures in Ireland had dropped to 73, and during the first ten months of the present year they had not amounted to more than 32. The improvement which is now in progress has been about equally felt in England and Wales, Scotland, and Ireland. TAR-DIPPED HURDLES.—Mr. George F. Wilson writes from Heatherbank, Weybridge :—" In these difficult times for farmers even the smallest improvement connected with their stock is of use. I therefore ask the favour of space to suggest the dipping of the hurdles used by them in tar. The notion was arrived at thus. In our wild garden at Oakwood, Wieley, I had to contrive shade and shelter for some plants on a hot hill-side. Close wattled hurdles answered the purpose and had the merit of taking nothing out of the soil, but ad the drawback of only lasting two or three years, as exposure to the weather rotted them, begin- ning at the part at the surface of the ground. We tried tarring with a brush, but could not get the 'tar into all the interstices; then proposed a heated tank for dipping in, but, before patting this up, on speaking to BOOM friends at the Walton Gasworks, it was proposed to dip them in a vessel there. I have now in use a number so tarred. They have the appearance of being black varnished, and are weather proof. An experienced farmer, well known and highly thought of in our neighbourhood—Mr. Shears, who farms the part of my small farm which I do not occupy—on seeing the black hurdles, said they would be desirable 'for farmers, and asked if he could get some dipped, and, on calling at the Gasworks at Walton-on-Thames, I found that it was proposed to dip for farmers, and that they had just dipped some hurdles different from mine fcr a neighbour to his great satisfaction." LANDLORDS AND AGRICULTURAL DEPRESSION.—I hear that at more than one club, in view of the approaching ter- mination of the year, tip committee have been requested by certain Irish members, dire sufferers from the state of affairs existing in their country, to allow the payment of their sub- scriptions to stand over until haPpier times. I understand, too, that there is a general disposition to comply with the request. A noblema who inherited a very fine property in the midland counties eleven years ago, containing some of the richest and best cultivated land in England, finds h m- self now, in these hard times of agriculture, with ten large farms thrown on his hands. The tenants on most of these farms were almost patriarchal, the leases having descended from father to tin for 150 or 200 years. The Due of Marlborough, the sale of whose valuable and really priceless library is making such a stir in the bibliological world, has at this moment more than 5,000 acres of land thrown on his hands. In Lincolnshire, many of Mr. Chaplin's and other gentlemen's farmers have been allowed to remain on to cul- tivate the land without paying rent at all.— World. ChovErt Sicietrass.—Dr. Linde holds with Kan, and in oppasition to Liebig, that clover sickness is due to parasites la the Boil, but he adduces no positive evidence of his asser- tion, except that he has found Pleospora herbarum in dead clover roots. He has conducted two Bets of field experi- ments for twelve years, and the story of them is what he tells, and it is only by inference that the parasite theory is at all supported. • In his first set of experiments, clover was grown without intermission for twelve years, while in the second set it alternated with field crops as in our Norfolk system. In both sets there were unneanured plots, the others being Immured with stable dung and other fertilisers. In the first set it was found that manuring (when considering' the average yield) had but little influence, and that in all cases clover sickness was apparent after a certain time. In the case of the nnmanured plot, it seemed to disappear after ten years. It was also found that whereas the unmanured plot required to be sown every three yeari, it was necessary to resew the others every two years. The yield on alt the " rotetion" plots was much higher than on the continuous plots. In the rotation plots, also, sickness VMS not visible; but on the continuous plots heavy manuring appeared to. produce a greater amount of sickness by causing a greater i y ield of clover. Hence, a larger amount of residue n the.. soil, which Dr. Linde avers produced a correspondingly , larger number of parasites. ,

One of the gnglish —Princ.esses; when her tutot, a bishop of the Church of England, said to her, "I Bad that my in- structions have made you but little better," replied, "Ah, but, my Lord, you do not know how much worse I should have been without them." Hugo Arnot one day, while panting with asthma, was almost deafened by the noise of a brawling fellow who was sellint oysters below his window. "The extravagant ras- cal !" said Hugo," he has wasted as much breath as would have served me for a month!"

About three pen., a goods train from Birmingham ran past an adverse signal into a stationary train in Spring Vale siding. The two engines and some of the trucks were smashed, and the debris piled across the line, the two drivers and two firemen marvellously escaping death. The line was completely blocked. Mails from Birmingham to the north, and from Stafford to the south, were sent via Walsall, and shortly before midnight the line was still blocked.

GIRLS WITTE MOIISTACHES.—" Yes," said an eminent physician, when the topic was being discussed at a dinner table after the ladies had retired. "When you see a dark woman with large bushy eyebrows which nearly grow to- gethert you may be pretty sure that she can grow an im- perial if she will only take the necessary pains. Hirsute adornments are not so frequent in young women, although they sometimes occur. A girl often has a heavy growth of down upon the upper lip or the chin. It annoys her, and she keeps feeling it and pulling it continually. Perhaps she endeavours to clip it with scissors, or in some cases to shave it away. The result is a heavier growth next time, which becomes so prominent that it must be removed. The most frequent place where the hair makes its appearance is on the upper lip or chin, although it sometimes appears or the side of the face, and even on the throat. As a general thing, I believe those bearded women who are advertised by shows are frauds; but in the course of my practice I have seen more than one woman who could raise a heavy beard if she only wished to cultivate it." "Do many women shave? Why, yes, a great many more than is generally supposed. They hide the traces that the shaving leaves with heavy doses of powder and plaster. Whenever you see a lady, especially it she be middle-aged, wearing a heavy coating of lily white, one of the conclusions is that she has been shaving, although it is not the only inference. One thing is certain, a lady who shaves must use powder in large quantities, and there are many ladies who shave." SLEEPING IN THE BASEMENT.—A paper of mine, pub., liehed in Good Words a few years ago' had an immediate and direct influence on this question of sleeping-places in basements. I wrote on the iniquity of that process with no unsparing hand, and on the principle of Jerome, "If an offence come out of truth, better is it that the offence come than the truth be concealed," I told the naked truth—not, I fear, in all its nakedness, but sufficiently to bring people to The result has been good to the extent of reform in some large houses, and some small ones also, so that many basements formerly packed with servants in darkness and damp are now left to ventilate through the night with pure air, instead of being ventilated by the emanations from the skin and the lungs of human beings. I now want to go a step farther, and to urge upon every householder never to let any human being sleep in the basement of the house at all. Steeping there is bad not only for the Bleeper, bat for the residents who sleep above, for the air of the basement ascends into the upper rooms, and is diffused there, to reach Probably the most fortunate, but not altogether fortunate, sleepers in the true sleeping-rooms of the dwelling. I make this criticism only in relation to a house where the base- ment is below the earth, or where it is closely confined by surrounding walls. There are positions, as at the sea-side, where in a house built on, not under, the earth, the bed- rooms may be well situated on a ground floor well raised from the earth. Of these houses lam not speaking, but of the bedroom under ground in the crowded town or city. If there be a room at the bottom of the house, I should advise that it be made use of as a room for occupation during the day, and at no time as a dormitory.—Dr. B. TV. Richard- son, F.R.S., in Good Words.

A dense fog prevais in many parts of the country on Saturday, and unfortunately resulted in ,accidents to ship- ping and loss of life. At Chester the body of a gentleman was found in the canal. At Brierley Hill three persons walked into the Birmingham Canal and were drowned. A number of other persons also fell into the canal, but were rescued. At Dudley station a man named Thos. Williams was killed while fog-signalling. On the Mersey the Wal- lasey ferry steamer, carrying a number of persons to market, came into violent collision with a barque anchored in the ferry track. The barque's boom swept the upper deck of the steamer, carrying away the whole of the rail, and injur- ing the man at the wheel. A second collision occurred shortly afterwards, the ferry-boat Mayflower running foul of the Russian convict steamer Nishni-Novgorod at anchor, and sustaining such damage that she bad to be beached. The passengers, men going to their work, were taken off in small boats. Ma. GLADSTONE AND HIS CONSTITUENTS—At a meeting in Dalkeith on Tuesday night, at the opening of a Liberal club, the following letter was read from Mr. Gladstone :—To Provost Mitchell. llawarden Castle, December 5, 1881. My dear Sir,—As some time may still elapse before I have an opportunity of addressing my constituents in person, I avail myself of the occasion offered by the opening of the Liberal Club at Dallceith to send my hearty good wishes on the occasion, and to assure you and your coadjutors that I have not forgotten the marked encouragement which I re- ceived from the inhabitants of the town at the period pre- ceding the last election, in a degree nowhere exceeded in the county of Midlothian. The manifestation which then took place had no exclusive reference to an individual or an occa- sion, and I rejoice to See in the meeting about to.take place a new indication of the enduring and unalterable attach- ment of the people of Scotland to the Liberal principles which the Administration they so largely contributed lo bring into power has laboured to the best of its ability to promote. In no way could, this celebration be made more effectual than by its being placed under the presidency of one so respccted as yourself.—'l remain, my dear sir, yours faithfey, W. E. GLADSTONE. TIIE Ben TaeneoaOF AMERICA.—" Amurica is a big fact," said an American, and no one will gainsay the proposition. The Americans delight in big things; they have the biogest rivers, the biggest trees, the biggest cities, the biggest fires, the biggest successes, and the biggest failures of any people in the world. As one of them harnourously said, when making fun of the weaknesses which are always an index of strength, "Our country has more lakes, and they are bigger and deeper and clearer and wetter than those of any other country. Our railcars are bigger, and run faster and pitch off the track oftener, then in any other country. Our steam- boats carry bigger loads, are longer and broader, burst their boilers oftener, and send up their passengers higher than in any other country," and so on. But this, of course, is "high falutin'." We shall, however, enjoy, as we tarry in the cities of the New World, the healthy humour of the people, which crops up everwhere and in everything; and is relished as much as maple-sugar or stewed clams. We shall try to see the American as be sees himself, and if we do not take ex- actly the same view of him as " half horse and half alligator, with a dash of earthquake," we may see him as "the child of Nature and of freedom, destined to lick all creation."— From "Cities of the World," Part .T., for December.

A gentleman told me of many farms he knew now tenant- less—of farms let formerly at 30s. vacated as impossible at that rent, and refitted for another tenant, if one should offer, but, none offering, relet to the just outgone tenant at lees than half his former rent. Of cases, too, where land worth hitherto 255. an acre is offered two years for nothing, the rent afterwards to be .E 1 an acre. "Now is the time to buy land or to hire it, as it seems to me," he said. " The younger generation have a better chance than their fathers had, if they have pluck enough to take it; and with the change of law now imminent, they ought not to fear." "Yon refer to the coming enactment of compulsory tenant right V" I said. "Of course I do. That and the abolition of the law of distress will be the two best things for landowners that you can name." " Ah t perhaps you agree with Professer Hunter and Mr. Howard, and the other leaders of the Farmers' Alliance, about their Land Bill." "Oh, they're all right," he said, "they know well enough they'll get what they want, and a good job too. They aim high enough to hit the mark they want to make. Com- pulsory tenant right will satisfy the Alliance,' and so it ought." "So it seems to me it ought; but I am not so sure as you appear to be that it will, though what they would get by empowering a tenant to sell his tenant right in the open market, I can't see. It seems to me that they would in like manner just empower the landlord to let the tenancy of his land to the highest bidder—the very scandal against which all good tenants hitherto have cried out. I don't see how the tenant can be empowered in the way they propose with- out it being understood as an invitation to the owner to do likewise. But perhaps after all it will be better so—the open market and the bare commercial principle being alike the resource and the guide of both." "I am in constant business relations with landowners all over this country," said my friend; "and I hear their side of the case. 'l'm all for freedom of contract,' they say. Not you,' I exclaim. Suppose now you offer use a piece of business to transact on the understanding that I receive £lOO to do it: do you think that that would stand? When the work was ,done you would soon learn otherwise. My bill for £lOO would not stand in any court. It would be taxed and recalculated and recast according to the legal rate of charges. Freedom of contract! Why, there is com- pulsory tenant right already. And when your tenant leaves you he receives for what he leaves the regular allowance which custom of the country, having the force of law, awards him, whatever may have been the bargain. Free- dom of contract! Why, you can't take a cab in the street but you know that the bargain you would make is already made for you by the law, and nothing but the legal rate can be exacted. Freedom of contract is not so universal as you think. We shall have tenant right liberally valued and , compulsorily established, you may depend upon it very soon. And you and your tenants will continue better Mende than ever—the land is in a wretched condition of impoverishment for want of it. Here are thousands of fat beasts imported every week, millions of cwts. of food each month, which at the price they make undoubtedly would repay an English producer. Why do they not come of English soil? The ' . land is net half cultivated. The want of industry and cap- ability, and capital and brains, out of which our present half-hearted agriculture has come, has these two things at , the bottom of it—the lam Of distress and the lack of security , for the tenant's capital." It was a solicitor in large practice who was speaking. "On the latter point I entirely agree with you," I said. " That is true at once, and in the very outset, and the for- mer also, no doubt, is in the long run mischievous all round, but not immediately, except to the capable tenant, who has his rent raised by competition with the incapable tenant." "It is mischievous at once to landlords, too," said the other. "It is an injury to the owner as well as to the culti- vator. Oh,' says a losing tenant, who cannot pay, 'you need not press; you are safe enough. Though all the other creditors should fail you are right enough. It'll all go to pay you at the last, even when I can go on no longer. You had better give me another chance.' And that is what Lord Brabourre calls enabling landlords to befriend a tenant. The whole system is mischievous. Rent should be like any other debt—safe, because paid when due; and the business of farming should stand upon the same lines as make other investments profitable.—elyricultural Gazette. During the ten nooks ending 31st October, 1881, this country imported among other food from abroad : Articles. Quantities. Declared value. Butter Cheese cwt. 1,605,233 £4,550,601 Eggs great hundred 5,421,652 £1,981,918 Is this creditable to our farmers? Is not dairying in this country c suable of such a development as to very largely diminish the above items represPnting as they do such enormous some paid to foreigners for what we can ourselves produce? Further, are not our thousands of farm yards competent by better management to earn the vast sum now paid for eggs to the small farmers of the Continent? We will first deal with the subject of dairying, on which Mr. G. M. Allender, the managing director of the Ayles- bury Dairy Company, read a paper at a recent meeting of the Central Farmers' Club, coetaining most valuable in- formation to those interested in the increased supply of dairy produce. The paper and the discussion which suc- ceeded it showed the great strides which have been made in this depaetment by a few of our most intelligent farmers, not only in the dairy appliances and machinery used, but as to what wonderful results in the shape of increased quantity and quality of milk can be achieved by the judicious selection and breeding of cows, and their being I well fed with suitable food, in fact the hints and ideas given I are no valuable, that as the object of these articles is to be as instructive as possible, and to tet people' thinking we give an epitome of Mr. Allender's paper. He said that id a -- four *mere ago be bad stated "Dairy farming in Eng- land has undoubtedly been neglected," but since that time not only has the Royal Agricultural Society of England made dairy work a special feature at the four last meetings of the society, but nearly all the other important associa- tions have "gone in for dairying." Dairy appliances and machinery of which we had no idea four years ago are now in common use. At Bristol, in 1878, we first heard that efforts were being made in Germany to devise a machine, by the aid of which the cream should be rapidly removed from milk by centrifugal force. Now, we have mechanical separators of at least five different forms. To such per- fection have these machines now been brought that the separated milk frequently contains as little as 15 15 per cent, of fat, and the cream can be so perfectly freed from milk that it will make as much as 18ozs. of batter to the quart of cream, whereas cream obtained by other methods seldom yields more than Hoes. (11b.), and very frequently much less. With reference to the question whether we produce milk either in proper quantity or quality, Mr. Allender does not think we do either the one or the other. He believes that the milk yielded by the number of cows now kept might be increased by at least one-third, if more attention were paid to selection. He was not aware whether the late Mr. Car- rington left any record of the milk yield of his cows, but Mr. Carrington agreed with the late Mr. Harrison, of Glou- cester that 550 gallons might be taken as the average yield of a good ordinary cow between calving and calving and Mr. Jenkins (Royal Agricultural Society, Hanover Square) quoted a yield of 700 gallons per cow, proved by carefully kept records at a farm in Denmark, and Mr. Allender ex- pressed his own belief four years ago that a well-selected herd of cows, dairy shorthorns, well-housed and welhfed, would average 900. gallons per cow in the milking year, (say 40 to 45 weeks). That the latter figure is within the mark is now proved by the very valuable record kept by Mr. Tie- dall, of West Farm, Epsom. The returns which Mr. Tisdall has been able to furnish are the most complete hitherto kept in this country, and very many thanks are due to him for this most valuable information. Twenty-five cows in milk ten to eleven months—say therefore about 43 weeks—gave an average of 885 gallons each, and that in several cases the actual yield of milk from individual cows reached 1,000 and 1,100 gallons in the ten months, many of them continuing to yield milk in good quantities for a further period of two I months. The most splendid herds have been brought to their present state of perfection by the care and attention bestowed by intelligent observant men on the selection of "the fittest." Why ehould not similar means be applied to improve the milk producing power of all cows? Mr. Tie- dall has for years carefully noted the yield of each cow at each milking, and. Mr. Allender thinks every farmer ought to do the same. If done he thinks everyone will find he has a cow that, compared with the others, is a beginning towards a little mine of wealth. A farmer who keeps cows that only give 400 to 450 gallons per cow stands to lose money, but it is his own fault that he keeps cows which are not only bad milkers, but which he feeds in an injudicious manner. On the other hand, a farmer who has a lot of 700 or 750 gallon cows gets on well, and if with more care as to selection and feeding the yield could be got •up to 900 or 1,000 gallons, a very handsome profit would be the result. Mr. Allender's advice to farmers is "if you keep cows, keep the best you can and feed them well." Cows should have a regular supply of clean, wholesome water, and every animal ought to have access to a large piece of rock salt, for salt is a positive necessity to a cow, and if withheld the quantity of milk will be lessened and probably its keep- ing quality impaired. Much valuable information was also given of the best kind of food for milking cows, and the most effective manner of making butter; while on the sub- ject of marketing butter he showed the great superiority of the French in sending their butter in a more marketable con- dition. Largely owing to this no doubt in ten years our imports of butter have risen from £8,000,000 to £12,000,000 sterling. What do these figures show? Take last year's returns of 2,326,305 met. or £12,141,034—equal to £3,325 per day. To produce this quantity of butter nearly 1,200,000 cows would be needed. Certainly the countries in which these cows are kept have no special advantage either in climate or Boil over ours—no great advantage over us in the value of the animals, or of labour and the cost of transport against them,—and yet there is the fact that a product of daily consumption, the fresher the better, and that could be produced in this country certainly as well, if not better, than in any other country Irt the world, comes here in these enormous quantities to feed our people, not only patting money into the pockets of the foreign farmer, . but paying a handsome commission to two or three large mercantile houses who have a finger in every cwt. hoported. What is the answer to this question? It is this, and this only. Foreign butter—whether it be fresh from Normandy or Brittany, or salt from Denmark or other Countries—comes in a more marketable form. The process by which this is arrived at is simple, and could be easily carried Out by us. Mr. Allender asks—Will we do it? That is the question.

Agents of the large houses in Normandy, such as Messrs. Bretel and others, attend the local markets, buy the butter from the farmers, who in their own interest attend to the rules laid down by the buyers. It is then carted to the stores or factories, and there put through a machine; so that instead of having 1,000 different lots varying from 201bs. to 501bs. each, they turn out many tons per day of precisely the souse sample. This, instead of being packed' in baskets, rough cloths, and perhaps newspapers in the English style, is put into boxes, each holding 241bs. in 2113 e. rolls neatly made and nattily papered, and if you look at 1,001 boxes you cannot tell " t'other from which." Of these boxes hundreds of thousands come over annually. The re- sult is that if this butter is not any better than that sent to market by English farmers it commands a higher price and more ready sale, because it is in a more marketable ' condition.

Air. Allender suggests that instead of each farmer making once or twice a week his two to ten dozen of butter' they should work together and make amongst them from 20 to 50 dozen per day, which would be of the same quality and appearance throughout, and enable the retailer to purchase direct their produce with as little trouble as he now buys foreign butter. A. Mr. Carrick has started a butter dairy on a large scale near Carlisle. He buys milk to a very large extent, and has already a most prosperous business. The demands of his customers already exceed his supply, and he lately had to refuse an offer of Is. 9d. per lb. for 5001bs. a week. In Devonshire a dealer is buying butter in the local market, re-working it, and sending out large quanti- ties of an equal sample. Machines for this purpose are now to be obtained, and it is a business well worth the attention of energetic men. Bo much for the possibilities of dairy farming in this country, and we all know what room there is for improve- ment.

And now we come to the question of pktry. In general -poultry is regarded as a very subordinate branch of rural economy, and most farmers deem it beneath their attention, or fancy that they have not time to attend to it, and often look on tee feathered inmates of their farmyard almost as a nuisance, because of their invasion of the fields. It may safely be asserted that there is no good reason for this, and that poultry properly cared for would always be a source of profit. The farmyard affords great advantages for the keeping of poultry, and the increasing demand of the market promises a safe return. The North of France and Pome- rania exceed all other parts of Europe in poultry keeping, which there Is not unfrequently the leading object of hus- bandry, and the traffic in the products of the poultry yard Is on a truly great scale. But what do we find in our own country? The English farmer, as a rule has no system in his poultry keeping. He has made no advance in his ideas. He keeps 60 or 100 hens of no .particular breed—thorough mongrels, in fact—mostly advanced in years up to six or seven, and the majority of them have long seen their best days. He feeds them on inferior or refuse corn, under the impression that they thereby cost him nothing, and they roost where they like. The hen-house gets cleaned out— well, sometimes—say once a year, whether it wants it or not, and it is usually in a shocking state enough to send a professional poultry-keeper into hysterics. There is no proper provision for nests; the fowls lay where they like, and the result must necessarily be that some eggs are either lost, stolen, or broken. A person who understands poultry, having the accommodation which se' farmyard and buildings afford, would be able to make a handsome priafit, after pav- ing the farmer & good rent. If a farmer wishes to make the most of his farm he will pay attention to poultry. He should commence with good stock, both as to age and breed, and see that they are properly attended to, like anything else. There must be every autumn a proportion, at least, regidarly replaced by young birds hatched in the spring of the same year. ' If this Is neglected, an empty egg basket during winter will eat up all the summer's profits. They ought to have a proper house, which should frequently be thoroughly cleaned out and lime-washed. Cleanliness in a hen-house. Is, decidedly profitable. The manure collected daily, and kept in a dry place, is in great demand by all nurserymen and gardeners who know its value. it fetches from ss. to 75. per cwt.' and is considered to average about 91 to is. per annum for each fowl. The hen-house should be pro- vided with suitable nest boxes, and perches at the proper height, and of the required width. The fowls should not be neglected in the winter months, when they are of the most value as layers, and when the profit should be the greatest. They then require additional warmth, like any other living thing, and this can be supplied to a great ex- tent by food. In winter they' have a meal about four o'clock, before going to roost, and to expect them to go without food until seven or eight next morning—a period of about 16 hours—is a great mistake. There should be a system of night feeding in winter, so that the birdo would have food enough to carry them on well to the morning. In summer, of course, they can easily be fed three times, say at 6 a.m., 2 o'clock, and at eight o'clock at night. Such a system Would wonderfully increase the number of eggs, and would not be found to involve very mach labour, which would be imply repaid. A good ordinary hen ought to lay 120 eggs in the year, and, if good laying breeds are se- lected, there ought to he an average of fully 150, whilst G-ame or ilamburghs will exceed 200 per annum. Of course good management is supposed, and a regular renewal of young stock. The prices obtained for fowls for eating pur- -1 poses in our large towns should cause farmers to turn their attention to the raising of chickens also. Mr. Wright, of Kingsdown, Bristol (a gentleman of great experience in poultry), is of opinion that it is to the farmer that poultry breeding on a large scale more especially comends Itself; and it may be pursued most successfully on either of two quite distinct syktems. A largo number ma ybe kept all through the year, and a portion of the farm—say one-fourth—per- manently appropriated in regular ration to their use, the fowls being removed to fresh ground every year. Or, on the other hand, a moderate breeding stock only may be per- manently retained, but a large number of chickens reared ire% %bent every season, which should be sent to the fields as soon as cropped in travelling houses mounted on wheels. There the chickens will speedily get fat at very little expense, and may be killed off for the market. The first plan is most suitable for la-ge faraaers with good business and administrative 'capacity; the last will be best adapted for smaller holdings. But Other system will not only yield a handsome profit in Itself, but greatly lone& the other produce, both by manuring the ground and by retiaoving the myriads of worms and insects very injurious to the growing crops. Indeed, considering the ravages yearly committed on every tam by these tiny pests, it is most astonishing that, instead of the bungling method of extermination at present em- ployed, the farmers of England do not have recourse to the philosophical and lucrative remedy which nature has pro- ilded. As to breeds, Dorkings should not be kept when eggs are the principal object, nor Brahmas when dead poultry is the end in view. If only one breed is desired, Hondans will be best, with a few Brahma hens for hatching and crossing. It is on the farm poultry ought to be most profitable; and in such circumstances, Mr. Wright considers every well- chosen stock fowl should represent a clear profit of five shillings per annum; whilst he is quite sure chickens will yield a much heavier weight of meat for the same outlay than any other stock whatever. His opinion is that the time is fast approaching when this will be generally recog- nised, and then, and not before, will poultry-breeding occupy Its legitimate position in the general economy of agriculture. There is an -equal want of management of ducks, which have the reputation of "eating their heads off." Is France, where duck-raising is conducted on a proper system, which has been proved by experience to be the best, the small farmers derive a considerable income from this source alone. „Bees are made a source of profit by people who under- stand them thoroughly, and an increased knowledge and systematic management by farmers would be attended with similar results.

Lastly, there is the question of fruit, to which feemers might turn their attention with advantage. Throughout most of Central Europe, where neither the soil nor the climate is in any way superior to our own, fruit trees are planted by the farmers and cottagers with.judicious care and discrimination in their fields and gardens. In an ordi• nary season they gather abundance of luscious fruit, not only enough to supply their domestic wants, but also to send large quantities to market, from which they realise an acceptable addition to their income. This is all done with- out losing a square yard of ground that could be profitably devoted to any other food crop. The trees are planted along roadsides, on the margins of the fields, in the hedge- rows, and in other odd pikes and corners, where they occupy ground that cannot be conveniently or profitably cultivated. In conclusion, many of our farmers evidently require educating in the latest discoveries in their own business; their labour must be more intelligently directed, they must be determined to take advantage of all their opportunities, and there must bea development of economical management in every department of farniing. Nothing ism insignificant as to be unworthy of attention, and the time has now arrived when the English farmer must put his best foot first.

div.head: YOREIGN INTELLIO-ENCE.
div.p: YOREIGN INTELLIO-ENCE.

report that plans and papers of great strategical Marshal Moltke has given a positive centred:Alma to the joportance had been stolen from the office of the General Staff. A "mysterious robbery" from the Offices a the Germ,zn General Staff is exciting a sensation at Berlin. Plans and papers of great strategical importance were, it seems, stolen about three weeks ago, and all efforts to discover the thief have been in vain. The actual number of the persons who perished in the fire at the Ring Theatre, Vienna, is still unknown. The estimates vary every day and the total, which was given at 580 OD Monday, is now Increased to 917. The exact truth may never be known. Further investigation reveals an almost- incredible amount of supineness and absolute Stupidity OR the part not only of the persons connected with the theatre, but of all those whose duty it was to save life and extinguish the fire, It is distinctly alleged that if the firemen had attended to the frantic entreaties of persons who had escaped from the theatre they might have penetrated into the galleries and saved scores, if not hundreds, of lives. The funeral of large numbers of the victims took place on Monday, and was attended by vast crowds. The official inquiry into the conduct of the police and firemen of Vienna during the burning of the Ring Theatre has established charges which Dtherwise would be simply incredible. It is no exaggeration to say that these,men are guilty of the deaths of hundreds of the miserable victims who were struggling vainly for their lives in the galleries, whilst the besotted officials in the street were superciliously disregarding the agonised entreaties of those who knew the real state of the case and were imploring them to hasten to the rescue. The rumour goes that the Grand Chamberlain of the Imperial Household has resigned in consequence of having received a sharp reprimand from the Emperor, who found that the too-zealous dignitary had sent a message or condolence to the manager of the Ring Theatre. The i number of the victims of the calamity s now generally estimated at 850. The end of the Guiteau trial Is, as yet, afar off. Tho pro- ceedings are fast verging upon the ridiculous, through the extraordinary latitude which is allowed, not only to the accused but also to the medical "experts," whose definitions of insanity would be amusing it they were intelligible. One of the "mad doctors" described Guiteau as a "moral mon- strosity with imbecility of judgment." Another said that in his opinion Guiteau was not depraved, but was a martyr to his sense of public duty. The criminal raved furiously in the dock, and the audience became so excited with horror and disgust that cries of "Shoot him now" were raised. The gaoler under whose care Guiteau has been placed has received a warning that it is intended to bilis up the part of the prison in which the assassin is lodged with dynamite.

-TRADE NOTES. On Monday, a mass meeting of the North Wales colliers was held on the Wrexham racecourse to consider what action should ha taken in view of the unsatisfactory relations ex- isting between themselves and their employers. After some preliminaries had been disposed of, it was proposed and seconded "that the interests of . the North Wales ners be left irr the . hands of the dele- gates already appointed, excepting in cases of an unusual course of action by the masters, when the delegates are to be further instructed by their constituents." An amendment to thiti was proposed to the effect that this meeting does not give such power to the delegates. The original resolution was, however, carried by a very large majority. The delegates will hold a meeting shortly to take into consideration the reply expected from the masters, to whom the resolution passed on Tuesday will be submitted. The steamboat men and fishermen engaged in the North Shields fishery, who have now been out on strike for nearly a fortnight, show no signs of returning to work upon the terms offered them by the owners, and their places are being taken by strangers.

BAIIIIOW-IN-FURNESS, MixlDAY.—There is practically no change to note in the condition of the hematite pig iron trade. The demand is fully maintained for all qualities of Bessemer iron, and forge qualities are also in the fullest request. Prices show no change. No. 1 Bessemer stands at 102 s. 6d. per ton at works or f.0.b., and No. 3 forgo at 60s. per ton, but several makerp decline to sell even for forward delivery. The output of the works is very large, and only a small portion of the furnaces are out of blast. Theoutput averages 32,500 tons per week. Deliveries are very heavy, but shipping, owing to bad weather, has been quiet. Ship- builders are very busy. Engineers and ironfonnders are doing a steady trade. LANCASHIRE, WEDNESDAY.—In the coal trade of this dis- trict a rather better tone has been noticeable during the past week. The change in the weather has had the effect of bring, beg more orders to the collieries for house-fire classes of fuel, and the market has shown rather more firmness. But al- though sellers are not quite so anxious to press sales as they were a week or so back, there are still large supplies of coal offering in the market and to clear off surplus stocks comparatively low prices arebeing taken for prompt delivery whilst short time continues to be worked at many of the Lancashire collieries. For house-fire coals at the pit mouth prices are about Os. 6d. to 10e for best qualities, 7s. ad. to Ss. for seconds, with common sorts offering at 6s. 61 to 7s. per ton. The common classes of round coal, although not so much affected by the weather as the better sorts, are also plentifnl notwithstanding that for iron-making and steam purposes there is a tolerably good demand, and for steam and forge coals comparatively low prices as compared with those quoted a month back are being taken, common Lancashire coal being obtainable at the pit mouth at from ss. 6d. to Os. per ton. For engine classes of fuel there is a fairly good demand, and for these prices are maintained, good slack being if anything rather scarce in the market. For good burg' at the pit mouth the average quotations are about 4s. Dd. to ss. 3d.. for good slack 45. to 4s. 3d., and for common sorts about 3s. to 3s. 6d per ton. The shipping trade continues dull, and Lancashire steam coal is offered, both at Liverpool and Garstoni at low figures. Coke in good demand, especially for iron-making purposes, and prices are firm at late rates. In the iron trade a tolerably large business has been doing during the past week, and there has been a further upwa-d movement in prices. Lancashire Makers of pig iron have advanced their quotations 2s, per ton, their price for delivery into the Manchester die- trict being now 31s per ton, less 21, for both forge and foundry qualities. At the advanced prices large Bales have been made for delivery over the first three months of next year, and Meal forge iron is now so scarce that makers have practically none to offer in the market, and with a con- tinuance of the present demand a further upward movement in prices is more than probable, whilst an increase of the output is in contemplation. Considerable transactions in Lincolnshire pig iron are also reported during the week at prices averaging about 50s. to 50s. Gd. per tcn, less 21 for delivery equal to Manchester, and an advance of is. Gd. to 1 2s. per ton upon these figures is now being asked. Derby- shire iron is also being quoted at considerably higher prices, but makers have recently been selling so heavily in Stafford- shire that they have now in many cases comparatively very 1 little to offer in this market. With the advance in the more local brands north country pig iron is now coming into the market more freely, and business is reported at prices rang- ing from 50s. to 525. Pd. net cash for Middlesborough foundry I and forge delivered equal to Manchester. Manufactured Iron is also stiffer in price, and local makers, who are mostly well soldjor the next three or four months, are not quoting • under £7 for bars delivered equal to Manchester, whilst merchants who have advanced 103. per ton during the week Iquote warehouse prices at £7 10s. per ton.

DEFECTIVE MEMOUT.—It is interesting, in a scientific sense, to trace the history of persons who labour under these curious defects of memory occurring in the premonitory or early tages of disease or decay. They will almost without exception, be found, on close scrutiny of their lives and experiences, to have exhibited at some previous period a want of capacity to learn, corresponding to their presentlack Of power to remember, and which is, in fact, the real cause of the trouble. Much harm is done and needless anxiety created by failure to recognise this fact. . These strange affections of memory; like -special errors of speech, are hastily set down as symptoms of the disease with which they are often found associated. They are no more symp- toms than great bodily wealiness is a symptom of consump- tion. They occur in the course ef disease, but they may I also occur in health, mut it is an unscientific and mischiev- ous fallacy to class them as indications of states they only I accompany, or of which perhaps they are the incidental effects or consequences. If there is no discoverabie evidence of a defect in the educational developmentof the mind which in mature life or advanced years exhibits a curious form of forgetfulness, the inquiry should be pushed farther back, and either in the previous or next but one preceding genera- tion a similar case will probably be found. Generally speak- ing, the maternal ancestry is most important in thu case of a male, and the paternal in that of a female sufferer from this defect. We have already seen how the physical, and therefore the mental, characteristics of the organism aro! transmitted, as the qualities of a plant are transmitted in its seed. PRESCOT BONIID OF GUARDIANS.

The usual fortnightly meeting of this Board was held on Thursday, at Whiston Workhouse, Mr. W. Tyrer presiding. There were also present, the Rev. T. Chambers, Messrs. Fidler, Hall, Meadows, Leatherbarrow, HobelL Jackson, Lowe, Ranson, Eatock, Buckley, Rowe, Penlieth, Syder, Fisher, Scotson, and Agnew; with Mr. S. H. Hartley (clerk).

WORKHOUSE MASTER'S REPORT. Mr. BICKNELL (the master) reported that there were 500 inmates in the Workhouse this week, as compared with 500 in the previous week, and 446 in the corresponding week of last year. There were 150 boys and girls at kirkdale schools. _
_ It was resolved that the usual Christmas treat to the in- mates should take place on Monday, the 26th instant.
A LUNATIC'S WINDFALL: HIS ENJOYMENT OF IT ENDANGERED.

The CLERK read a letter from Mr. Win. Swift, solicitor, of Liverpool, stating that a person named Winstanley, an in- mate of the Rainhill Asylum, and chargeable to some parish I in the Prescot Union, bad, he was informed, become entitled to the sum of £4OO (less costs) under the estate of his late son, which was being administered in the Chancery Court at Li% erpool. The Guardians might consider it desirable to ascertain what proportion of the £4OO they could receive and apply in aid of his maintenance at Ratak'll, and lithe Clerk would call at his office he would supply him with the information he had on the subject.—The CLERK remarked that Winstanley was admitted into the Asylum on the 10th May, 1870, and the amount paid by the Union for his maintenance up to the 30th September last was £293 Os. 7d. The Clerk acVed that the least the Guardians could do was to thank Mr. Swift for the information. (Hear, hear.)—The Clerk was authorised to take the necessary steps. —Mr. Rown said he thought Mr. Winstanley belonged to the Hale. He had been in the asylum a good many years. —Mr. FIDLER said be had great pleasure in proposing that the thanks of that Board be tendered to Mr. Swift for his attention to the interests of that Union.—Mr. MEADOWS seconded, and the motion was unanimously passed.

div.head: ROYAL VISIT TO MANCHESTER.
div.p: ROYAL VISIT TO MANCHESTER.

IThe Duke of Edinburgh, the Duke of Albany, and Plince Christian were cordially welcomed, on Tuesday, by the citizens of Manchester, on the occasion of their visit. Their Royal Highnesses arrived from London in the afternoon, and drove to the Athenteum, where the medallion portraits, lately subscribed for, of the three principal founders of that institution—Mr. Richard Cobden, Mr. William Langton, and Mr. James Heywood, F.R.S.,—were unveiled by the Duke of Edinburgh. At night the distinguished visitors, who were the guests of the Mayor, at the Town Hall, attended a grand soirée of the members of the Atheneum, the Duke of Edin- burgh presiding, held in the Free Trade Hall, with the view of creating an interest throughout the provinces in an insti- tution for the advancement of music, ranking in importance with the National Conservatoires on the Continent. The subject was treated under two heads—first, the aaesthetic and historical side of music, which furnished material for an able address by the Duke of Albany; and secondly, its prac- tical side, under which was included the difficulties and expense of musical education and the necessity of its being fostered by public aid. The latter was dealt with by the Duke of Edinburgh, who sought to enlist the sympathies of his audience on behalf of a Royal Academy of Music—in other words, a college of musicians, which should fie on a more permanent and extended basis than any existing institution and competent to teach and speak with authority; also that the institution so formed should be assisted by the public and be recognised and sub- sidised by the State. Prince Christian described the prac- tical steps which had been taken towards accomplishing the object aimed at, and mentioned that a charter for a Royal College of Music the petition for which was presented by the Prince of Wales some time ago, was still under the con- sideration of the Privy Council. The objects of the College, as described in the charter, were "the advancement of the art of music by means of a central representative body charged with the duty of private musical instruction of the highest class, and having a capacity to exereise a powerful influence on the cultivation, practice, and regulatiin of the art and science ot music; and further, having in view the promotion and supervision of musical instruction as may be thought most conducive to the caltivatien and dissemina- tion of the art of music in the United Kingdom." The charter contemplates the' foundation of scholarships, and also the reception, as pupils, of young persons who are desirous of obtaining the advantages of a strict collegiate course of musical training. The meeting was afterwards addressed by the Archbishop of York, Lord Houghton, the Bishop of Manchester, Sir F. Bramworth, and others.

div.head: LIBERALISM AT IVRTIIWICH.
div.p: LIBERALISM AT IVRTIIWICH.

A well-attended meeting of the Liberals of Northwich was held on Wednesday night, in promotion of the establish- ment of a Liberal club in the town. Amongst those present were Mr. G. W. Latham,Liberal candidate for Mid-Cheshire • Mr. Toinkiason, Liberal candidate for West Cheshire; and Mr. Evans Williams, M.P. for Radnor Boroughs.—Mr• LATHAM, in supporting a vote of confidence in the Liberal Government, said that the newspaper called by courtesy the leading journal, had complained that too much public speak- ing was going on in the country, but he did not think this complaint came well from a journal which devoted half of one of its sheets the other day to speeches of Lord Randolph Churchill, which bore internal evidence Of having bean printed from his lordship's own notes. (Laughter.) They knew how Lnportant it was for an absolute monarch to receive advice from his councillors. England was at present ruled ,by that mighty sovereign Demos, who could neither be assasinated nor disobeyed, and it was their duty to give him the best advice they could. That advice must be given by word of mouth, and, however some high-sniffling critics might sneer, Demos generally went pretty nearly right. He believed in the decision of the public as he believed in the decision of a jury. In -ninety-nine cases out of a hundred it was right; but both the public and a jury needed the direction of advocates and the summing-up of a judge. (Applause.) Therefore, he would say, let Lord Salisbury go en jeering; let Sir Richard Cross go on asserting; let the Right Hon. Jimmy Lowther go on bleating. (Laughter.) There was only one thing he would ask of them, and that was that they should tell the truth, and state plain facts, and these they would be ready to answer. (Cheers.) They were content to leave the verdict to the British public. A short time ago there was a meeting of their Conservative friends in that room, and he was told to read the speeches made on that occasion in order that he might answer them. Ile had done that duty, and a dreary task it was. (Laugh- ter.) From Dan to Beersheba all was barren. There was a little imitation of Lord Salisbury's sneering, of Sir Stafford Northcote's milk and water with a little mote sky blue added to it, and the major prophets of the party were quoted by the minor prophets; but anything good or new could not be found in the speeches. He was actally disappointed that he had nothing to answer. In one of the speakers on that occasion there was a fund of humour--not in himself, but in his speech. (Laughter.) That speaker was a reverend gentleman whom they would have expected to be serious and steady. He thought the admission of Mr. Bradlaugh to the House of Commons would be a rapid cause of the dis- establishment of the Church. (Laughter.) He (Mr. Latham) was no more in love with • crusading Atheist than that reverend gentleman; but that was not the vestion. A constituency, knowing what Mr. Bradlaugh was, bad chosen to elect him. The constituency was the fudge of his fitness, and, much as he hated Mr. Bradlaugh's opinions, he said the House of Commons was bound to admit him. tCheers.) The rev. gehtleman next went on to Fair Trade, and here he displayed a knowledge which was unexpected in one of his cloth, when he said he should not advise the country to go "nap" on a three-hand. (Much laughter.) He heard before this that there were a certain number of elder sons roaming about the Continent penniless, because they had not led trumps when they had five cards in their hands, but be never heard before that the depression of British trade was caused lay "going nap with a three-hand." (Laughter.) He should rather have thought it was owing to their playing those games the Conservatives knew better than anybody—" snap," "beggar my neighbour," and "cribbage." (Much laughter and applause.) Of these games they were particularly fond; while they knew nothing of "patience" and "commerce." (Renewed laughter and applause.) Referring to Conservative strictures with regard to the new rules to be imposed on the House of Commons, he said that Mr. Gladstone and Mr. Bright—to whom free- dom of speech had been as the breath of life—would be the last to impose rules which might curtail that freedom when they were in Opposition. Speaking of coming legislation, he said the first thing they must try for must be to get our system of local legislation amended. They needed to reform the present confusion of overlapping authorities, and to obtain representative county government, by which means they would be able to control their own money. The land question was demanding attention, and until thb country could see its way to con- tinuity of tenure, he would be glad to accept the Farmers' Alliance Bill as the best available, and whether the present Parliament passed it or not, he believed it wbuld be passed. (Cheers.) The towns were interested in the question, because to them it meant chop food. (Cheers ) The equalisation of the borough and county franchise was a question they in Northwich had a particular interest in. Many people fancied it was only necessary to draw up a bill of one clause enacting that the county. and borough franchise should henceforth be equal. But such a bill would render the borough franchise much narrower than it was at present, and they must have some settlement of the question as to whether the freeholdet must remain or go off the list entirely These and other questions ought to he seriously debated in such clubs as they were forming, and the Government should be made acquainted with their views on the subject. Liberal- ism might be summed up in one word—opposition to mono- poly. They would find that one monopoly supported another, and then if they destroyed ono after another ef these rotten faggots, they would eventually loosen the whole bundle, and would be able to cast the whole of them Into the purifying fire of reform. (Cheers.)—Addresses were afterwaals delivered by Mr. Tomkinson on the benefits of Free Trade, and by Mr. Evans %Mame, M.P., on the evils of obstruction. A vote of confidence in the Government was carried unanimously. Steps are being taken for the immedi- ate formation of a Liberal club. Mr. Tomkirson stated that over 1,000 Liberals had been added to the register in West-Cherhire, and they were ready to fight and confident of victory.

RUNCORN TAM O'SITANITRS V. SIMMS' CROSS ROVERS. —This match was played on the ground of the former on I Saturday, and resulted in an easy victory for the home I team. For the visitors Telling, Watson, and • Devonport showed themselves conspicuously, while for the home team Pownall, Wainwright, Howard, and Peacock played well. The score is as follows :—Tarn O'Shanters : Two goals, 1 I try, 5 touchdowns, and 3 dead balls. Simm's Cross: One disputed try and 1 dead ball. Teams :—Tana O'Sbanter : Full back, W. Seed (captain), Williams and Devonport ; half I backs, Smith and Huce ; forwards, Harrison, Dennet, Davies, I Ormon, Hunt, Felling, Evans, Watson, and Santley.

div.head: ST. HELENS WESLEYAN IMPROVE. MENT ASSOCIATION.
div.p: ST. HELENS WESLEYAN IMPROVE- . MENT ASSOCIATION.

The members of the Wesleyan Improvement Association on Wednesday night listened to an interesting lecture on " The English Revolution," by Mr. Thomas Brown. The Rev. W. G. Pascoe occupied the chair. The LEcnama said that in 1680 our ancestors saw fit to invite Charles 11. from his exile, and to restore unto him the throne of his fathers. The event was one of great moment. Would kingly tyranny revive? Would despotism come back with the crown and the tyrant's sore.? Would the Anglican Church be allowed to exercise a spirit of persecution to- wards her enemies? Had past struggles had a beneficial effect, and had they taught a useful lesson, so that the eon who was invited to take the crown would not step in the footsteps of his father from it had been taken? These were momentous questions, and one would think would receive due consideration by the men of those times. Alas, ip the exuberant state of the Restoration those matters were over- looked. Under the vigorous administration of Cromwell and the Commonwealth there had been many great restraints, which, however beneficial, were not liked by all. When the Restoration was complete a strong reaction took place, and the nation passed from one extreme to the other. Hav- ing described the character of Charles 11., who was a Roman Catholic, and enumerated some of the acts which had rendered his name obnoxious, Mr. Brown went on to say that the nation fast receded from the proud position which it had maintained daring the Commonwealth, and Popery was once more lifting up ita head. But the storm was again gathering, and ere long would burst in fury on the land. The Government daily become more odious, the old spirit took possession of the people, and they were again in earnest for their honour and their liberties—they were again alarmed at the growing power of the Church of Rome. Again Parliament became obstinate and resisted kingly authority. The king died in 1685, receiving the sacrament according to the rites of the Romish Church. He was succeeded by his brother as James the Second, a man who would rather break than bend, whose bigoted, violent, and obstinate disposition brought matters to a crisis. Charles the Second met the Lords of the Privy Council shortly after his proclamation, and made the following remarkable speech: —"My Lords,—Before I enter upan any other business I think fit to say something to you. Since it bath pleased Almighty God to place me in this station, and I am now to succeed so good and gracious a king, as well as so kind a brother, I think it fit to declare to you that I will endeavour to follow his example, and most especially in that of his great clemency and tenderness to his people. I have been , reported to be a man for arbitrary power, but that is not the only story that has been made of me; and I shall make it my endeavour to preserve the government both in Church and State as it is now by law established. I know the principles of the Church of England are for monarchy, and the members of it have shown themselves good and loyal subjects, therefor I shall always take care to defend and sup- port it. I know the laws of England are sufficient to make the king as great a monarch as I can wish to be, and as! shall never depart from the just right and prerogative of:the crown, so I shall never invade any man's property. I have often heretofore ventured my life in defence of the nation, and I shall still go RS far as any man in preserving it in all its just rights and liberties." The speech was an agreeable surprise to the Loris, and the nation was in ecstacies. Happy would it have seen for James had he kept to his promises. But be was a Stuart, and on that account we could scarcely trust his fair words. The lecturer then criticised the actions of James, and said that if James had had a spark of tenderness in his bosom, and desire 4 to treat his people with mildwes and gentleness, why was such a man as Judge Jeffreys introduced into the Cabinet, and made Chief Justice of the land ? His name was a foul blot on the page of English history, and had beco.no a proverb for blasphemy and brutality. He was a tool in the hands of James, and yet James could say of him—" That man has no learning, no sense, no manners, and more impudence than ten carbed street walkers." Contrary to his promise James departed from the just rights and prerogatives of the crown, and many times did he invade the rights of private indivi- duals; contrary to the rest Act he gave commissions to the army, and to the Roman Catholics, released all Romanists from penalties, and contrary to the constitution he prepared to form a standing army, a court of High Commission with Jeff rys at ,its head, collected Customs Duties without the sanction of Parliament, interfered with elections, and by means of French gold tried to secures servile House of Com- mons. The people were astonished and murmured, and so roused were they at the attempt to send eighty-five incum- bents to the tower, that they made a magnificent demonstra- tion. One of the bishops was a Cornishman, and throughout that county might be heard echoing on every hand— And shall Trelawney die, and shall Trelawney die, Then 20 00 Cornish boys will know the reason why.

They were pronounced "Not guilty" by the jury, and loud brans were heard all over London. Prince William of Orange was invited over, and William and Mary were declared King and Queen. The cause of civil and religious liberty triumphed once more, and tyranny and Popery were again swept from the land.—Remarks were made on the lecture by Mr. May, Mr. Ackerley, Dr. MeNicoll, and the chairman.
