div.head: ST. HELENS TOWN COUNCIL.
div.p: ST. HELENS TOWN COUNCIL.
The monthly meeting of this Council was held' on Wed- nesday, Dr. Twyford presiding. There ware ales present AM. Gamble; Councillors Brook, Jamison, Wil coal. Belsher E. Johnson, Massey.

div.head: RESIDENT ALKALI WORKS rtZSPECTOII.
div.p: RESIDENT ALKALI WORKS rtZSPECTOII.

The DEPUTY Town. CLERK read a letter which had been sent to the Local Government Board by the Town Clerk asking for the appointment an alkali works inspector ex- clusively for and residing in St. Helens. The letter pointed j out the importance of the alkali trade in St. Helens and thought the Board would be justified in making the appoint- ment.—The Local Government acknowledged the receipt of the receipt of the letter, and stated that the subject would receive the consideration of the Board.—The Council decided to forward the correspondence to Dr. Angus Smith, with the object of getting him to use his influence in favour of the appointment.

div.head: THE. INFECTIOUS DISEASE'S HOSPITAL.
div.p: THE. INFECTIOUS DISEASE'S HOSPITAL.

The Hospital Sub-Committee after inspecting the Hospital recommended that the floor be covered with linoleum, that a quantity of bedAclothing be obtained, that shelves be erected, &c.—The Council decided that the following scale of charges be adopted :-Is. per day for every patient whose wages do not exceed 20s. per week; and 3d. for every additional five shillings. This will not include medicine and medical attendance.—A conversation took place in respect to the ability of persons to pay in case there were three or four ill in the same family.
Mr. CRAIK said they could lower the scale after it had beeg fixed, but there might be some difficulty in raising it, so That it could stand as it was.

div.head: THE. WATER SUPPLY AT SUTTON HEATH.
div.p: THE. WATER SUPPLY AT SUTTON HEATH.

The subject of the water supply to the inhabitants of Sut- ton Heath came on again for consideration, the inhabitants having, some few weeks ago, memorialised the Health Com- mittee to give them a supply from St. Helens. The memorial stated that their only sources of supply were from the fields and ditches, the water from the two draw wells there being unsuitable for consumption. Mr. BROOK thought something should be done for the in- habitants, as it was evidently unsafe to drink the water now obtainable in the district.

- It was stated that the cost of extending the mains would be considerable. Alderman Gaunrz said that the statement of the inhabi- tants was manifestly incorrect. They said they had no wells, but that was not tree, as there were wells in the dis- trict; and seeing there was no complaint of any injury having resulted from the consumption of the water he saw no necessity for the Corporation taking any steps. Mr. MASSEY pointed out that there was a clear allegation in the memorial that the water from the wells was not suitable.

Mr. BROOK moved that the Surveyor be instructed to re- port at the next meeting as to whether the houses at Sutton Heath were provided with a proper stipply of water, and that he have the water of the district analysed. Alderman Groantz saw no reason why the Corporation should go to the expense of analysing the water, for they did not know how many samples would be taken. It was stated that the cost of analysing a sample of water would be one guinea. Alderman GAMBLE moved an amendment that' the memorialists defray the cost of one half of the expense. Mr. Enoox said the coat of the analysing of the water was BO small as compared with the importance of the subject, that really he did not think the committee ought to make such exactions, especially when the Council weat to such a great expense in other matters. Alderman GAMBLE B.iid he would withdraw his amend- ment.

div.head: REtORT OF CHIMNEYS.
div.p: THE REtORT OF CHIMNEYS.

..... The SURVEYOR said he had written to Roberts' Copper Works, St. Helene Lead Company, and St. Helens Chemical Company, asking the height of their works' chimneys, the diameter, and number of furnaces; but he had received no reply. Alderman GAMBLE stated that the resolution passed at the last meeting was to the effect that the Surveyor report on the height of the chimneys and generally thereon. Dr..Listisos said that was the resolution he proposed. The SURVEYOR said he had no right in the works except with the consent of the owners.

Alderman GAMBLE said what they wanted was the height of the chimneys as compared with other chimneys, and as compared with the height of the houses in reach of the smoke, so that the committee might be able to judge whether it was reasonable for them to insist upon the chimneys being raised. He did not see what they had to do with the num- ber of flues and furnaces.
The SURVEYOR said he was perfectly satisfied that one of the chimneys could not be raised, because it-bad not a suffi- cient amount of base. •
Dr. JAMISON said they had nothing to do with that; what they wanted was a comparison with the other chimneys. It was understood that the Surveyor would report at the next meeting.

div.head: MEDICAL OFFICER'S REPORT.
div.p: MEDICAL OFFICER'S REPORT.

"Samples of Eccleston Brook, taken by Inspector Will Ams at the usual places between Spray's Bridge and Messrs. Lyon's bottle works, are free of acid. Just below the latter 'Point the overflow from the canal into the brook contains acid, as shown by a sample handed to me by Inspector Houghton. At the same time sulphuretted hydrogen was present in the gasworks yard, probably evolved by the agency of the acid from the canal acting on sulphur. Hard- shaw Brook is free, though some acid is in a tsample of drain- age coming from the Globe Alkali Works. The drainage from the St. Helens Chemical Works is still acid, bat the strength is less and the stream is more moderate. The house at Broad Oak reported last meeting has just been repaired, but a door has been placed over the gap in the thatch, and the gable end has been plastered in places with waste from chemical works. It had better be closed." This was ordered to be done. THE HEALTH OF THE TOWN. Dr. Menem. reported:—" The health of the town is fairly good for the season, the mortality for the month being 2118, which is about the average of the year's mortality. An epidemic of measles and also of scarlet fever prevails, and fever is still prevalent in a sporadic form. The people of Sutton are dissatisfied with the water supplied to them. They complain of it being hard, and one ratepayer says it has affected his health."

div.head: OLD .SOHOLARS' TEA PARTY AT ST. -HELENS.
div.p: OLD .SOHOLARS' TEA PARTY AT ST. -HELENS.

—. ---•---- . i Al" very pleasing meeting was held in the Waterloo-street schoolroom on Tuesday evening. The Wesleyan ministers here determined to make an effort te bring as many old scholars t •-rher as possible, and the appearance .of the 03'—' . • • ' ' "-' gathering on Tnesday it ifaa a inaot that the effort had been eminently successful. An eitiellent tea was,provided, , and the tables were presided over bylmales. Afterwards there was a meeting held, at which there were present about 400 persons, many of whom had not been to Sunday school for years. There was also a large namber of young men at present attending, and engaged in Sunday school work. Prior to the commencement of the meeting the time was eccupied in singing popular hymns.-,The Rev. J. M. WALRISLEY said that soon after coming to St. Helens, Ilhd ' after the first Sunday he had the pleasure of occupying ths Wesleyan pulpit, he noticed that they had a large number of young men in the congregation who did not attend school. Thinking the matter over the following week his mind was impressed with the question. How Was it possible to get hold of these young men, and have a little free and pleasant talk with them upon the most important of all qaestious. After a while it struck him that they 'could be got at, and got together by means of a cup of tea. He maned the mat- 'ter to his colleagses, who agreed with the plan, and they took steps to carry it into effect. He afterwards mentioned

:he mater at the. leaders' meeting, and they very heartily took up the matter; in fact, some of the members emphati- cally said that they thought that there had not been quite so I much notice taken of the young men as there ought to have been. They thought that a meeting of that characterwould be productive of very great good. A committee was ap- pointed to give effect to the wishes of the promoters, and two excellent young men were appointed as secretaries,—Mr. J. J. Cook anti Mr. Alfred Jones. As the result of the de- liberations of the committee they were gathered together that evening. He was sure they would all accept the words of a hearty we/come, which in Isis own name. in the names of his colleagues, the stewards and local preachers of the Methodist Society of Cotham-streer and Park-road, he ex-. tended to them. They were delighted past everything to see their faces. Personally, he had always taken—and he thought he always should take, an interest in the-youmg men. He knew the difficulties that beset the path of young men, and-he always liked to be free with then,. Gienfleld starch was all verywell in it way, but it would not do for a thing of that sort: When a young man looked, upon his face, he wanted that young man to feel that he WMe looking upon the face of a friend, and he maid that he was only echoing the oentiments of 31r. Pascoe and. Mr. Crozier. Mr. Walmaley urged upon the young men the importance of giving their hearts to God while they were young, and to emphasize the advice he related incidents in connection with his own early lie. He was a Staffordshire man, and was brought up in Leek, sometimes, called the metropolis of the midland counties. When quite a boy Ile was apprenticed to a tradesman in Burnley, and those who had passed through the experience of the term of' life known as the term of apprenticeship would understand him when he entered into the feelings peculiar to that period of life. He knew something of the dangers, of the difficulties and diseouragements incident to a young man's life. He thanked God•that soon after he went to Burnley he was led to give his heart to Christ. That was about 31 years ago. The person to whom he was apprenticed was only a half-hearted Christian, and before he (Mr. Walmsley) was bound he made We, condition that he should go to class once a week. His mother came from Staffordshire to, sign- the indentures. The document was laid on the table, to be read over, but did not find the clause giving him power to attend class once a week, lie pointed this out to his master and said that he could uot sign his name unless it was in- serted. His master thought it was not necessary, but was- ultimately obliged to insert the clause. Through his in- fluence and that of another Christian young man in the same place, that half-hearted Christian was brought to see. the error of his lukewarmness. 41r. Walmsley concluded he- saying that religion had been his cemfurt in the day Of sorrow, his light in the day of darkness, and his strength in the day of weakness.—The Rev. R. Crozier, of Earlestown, the Rev. W. G. Pascoe, Messrs. W. B. Houghton Stubbs, and T. Waterworth addressed sense appropriate words to the. meeting. The addresses were earnestly delivered and were- listened to with rapt attention. An enjoyable and profitable, meeting was spent.

• NEWTON AND EARLESTOWN. We learn that the day-school scholars are to have as month's holiday from the 16th, in order to promote the abatement of the epidemics which have prevailed. FATAL RAILWAY ACCIDTINT.—A man named James Bate was killed on Saturday, at the signal box between Newton and Lowton Junction, while placing some fog signals on the line.

LIBERALS V. CoroEnv-arms. The billiard.match be- tween the Liberal and Conservative Clubs is being con- tinued in the club-room of the latter, who were on Tuesday night leading by one point. The sewering in High-street is finished, and it only re- mains now to enforce the bye-laws compelling property owners to lead their drains into it to ensure the health °fall the inhabitants of Newton as far as sanitary measures can ensure it.

IST. PErEn's CHURCH.—Sermoss were preached in the above church, on Sunday last, by the Rev. W. Crane, MA., (Rector of St. George's, Ilulme, and Canon Residentiary of Manchester, on behalf of the Society for the Propagation of the Gospel in Foreign Parts. IMPROVED Gas Lenrrs.—During the last week or two, the inhabitants of Newton and Earlestown have had an opportunity of judging of the superiority of the new gas- lamps and lights which have recently been placed at ass round points opposite the Church and Oak Tree Inn in New. ton, and Market-place, in Earlestown. It is Bray's Patent and is a most decided improvement in gas lighting. DEAN SCROOL Crtmarrv..Daring the week we have seen the Christmas report of the Manchester Grammar School, where the three scholars sent from Newton appear to keep up their reputation in place and position. In mathematics (H. G. Willis, M.A.) Woodcock is 12th, Harrison 17th, Limond 20th. In Latin Harrison is 10th,middie second form (second master). In drawing and writing (Z. Trichard and J. Jackson) the three stand in the same order, let, Bth and 12th (middle second form). In Divinity and English (C. E. Brown, 8.A., and L. H. Meller)Harrison 3rd, Woodcock sth, and Limond 6th. In French, same masters but separate classes for Harrison, and in the same order, sth, 6th and 7th, P. E. E. Barbier, master, form list, 4th, sth and 7th which is highly creditable to them all. EARLEFrrowle MUSICLL Soctierr.—As it has been deemed advisable to have only one concert this season and that one a thoroughly creditable one with the object of providing a change from the weekly rehearsal, the members decided to have a social evening on Wednesday, in the Wesleyan In- fante-school, to which each member was at liberty to bring a friend, and availed themselves of the privilege freely, there being as many present as the room would cornfortably hold. The society is in a prosperous condition considering that it has only been established this season. It consists of 36 members, and so far has secured seven honorary members and subscribers, viz.: Messrs. Charles Pillcingtou, B. B. Glover (Havdock), D. Davidson, .1. C. Wood, John Dick (Newton), B. Walker, and J. Roberts (Earlestown). Mr. P. M. Campbell is the president, Mr. John Hayes conductor, und Mr. Wm. Walton. honorary secretary.

FRODSHAM. ACCIDIttiT AT FRODSHAM Burnon.—On Tuesday evening at Frodsham Bridge, one of the shafts of Mr. Dignum's bread cart broke, and Mr. W. Dignum and Mr. Tinsley were thrown out of the conveyance, but -fortunately escaped with a slight shaking. The horse took fright, but stopped at Mr. Thomas Andrews, when it was found that the remaining shaft was also broken.

MR. STEWARD'S CHRISTMAS SALE.—The usual Christmas sale of fat stock was held by Mr. Steward at the Queen's Head Hotel, Frodstaam' on Thursday. On one occasion, when the late Lord Bishop of Lichfield bad spoken of the importance of diligent, painstaking pre- paration for the pulpit, a verbose young clergyman said, " Why, my Lord, I often go to the vestry even without knowing what text I shall preach upon; yet I go up and preach an extempore sermon, and think nothing of it." The Bishop replied, " Ab, well, that agrees with what I hear from your people, for they hear the sermon, and they also think nothing of it!" The Vice-Consul at Cherbourg telegraphed on Thursday to-the Foreign Office that on Wednesday morning a fisher- man of that port, while at sea 20 miles from the English coast and SO miles from the French coast, between Cape La Hogue and Alderney, sighted an object resembling a balloon floating on the water. Searchers were at once despatched with the fisherman to the spot. Telegrams have been re- ceived at the Admiralty and by the President of the Balloon 1 Society confirming this report, but up to the time of going , to press no information had been received of the result of i i Thursday's search. _ _.

The National Miners' Conference was resumed at Birming- ham oa Thursday; Mr. Burt, M.P., presiding. It isss resolved to request a deputation of the Mining Associations to confer with the Miners' Associations of Great Britain with a view loan advance of 10 per cent in wages. It was urgent that miners were thus doing only what the ironworkers had done. The next subject was the formation of a National Federation of Miners. Mr. Crawford pointed out bow by organisation the legal position of the miners had beets improved. Mr. Wood (Yorkshire) thought the org!tnisation should embrace political ends also. A resolution in favour of the proposed federation was carried.

In conclusion, Mr. Eglinton said: And now the voice that has spoken to you, dear friends, with such acceptance from this pulpit is speaking to you from his grave in that sunny land of such varied memories, for "Re being dead yet speaketh," enforcing all the lessans he taught YOU in life; and surely that voice, though mute, shall not now speak in vain. Already I have learned that the fact of his burial in that ancient city has been an inspiration to some whose spirits drooped amid causes of depression in missionary work; and it may be that, as in the case of Machpelah and Rachel's tomb, indicating the future of the Promised Land, so that humble grave, holding the remains of him whose memory is dear to you andlo me, may lead to the consecrated service of youthful hearts. and lives to the evangelisation of that Italy which is now united and free, and awaiting a purer faith, receives to her capital and provinces the ambassadors of Rim who is the wearetil the triple crown, having the keys of hell and death, in tiii6le—rinde -ire "oar f.iinefs, who opens and no man shuts, and who, in his own time—too early as it seems to us; but the "due season" has opened to him the &Az of his Father's house—the house of mans mansions—and ,smilingly welcomed him to the city of everlasting habitations. The house of eur Father above, . The palace of angels oriaod. May we follow him as he followed Christ. Amen. The Rev. J. MEMORIAL SERVICE AT WARRINGTON. THE LATE REV. F. S. HAGEN. It is on very rare occasions that the spacious edifice known as Bold-street Wesleyan Chapel, is filled by such a vast con- gregation as that which assembled there on Sunday evening last. The occasion for this unusual attendance was the holding of what was designated a "Memorial service for the late Rev. F. S. Hagen,"—a service peculiar to the Metho distic body—and the great assembly, composed of members of the various Methodist churches in Warrington and neigh- bourhood, demonstrated in the most effective manner the esteem which the deceased minister had won during his brief sojourn amongst them. When the service' commenced the chapel was comfortably filled in every part, but the congre- gation was afterwards greatly augmented, and the late ar- rivals had to be accommodated with seats placed in-the aisles. The pulpit was draped in black, and the choir and many members of the congregetion were attired in mourning. The superintendent minister, tale Rev. John Eglinton, preached the unarm from Hebrews iv. P. "There re- maineth therefore a rest to the people of God." At the con- clusion, the rev, gentleman said it was to be regretted that, so fares they could discover, Mr. Hagen had not left any record of his inner* life, but the consistency and calm radiancy of his outward course gave constant evidence of the spirit enshrined within. The son of a father who was an accomplished and gifted minister of Jesus Christ in their own church but whose course was singularly unobtrueive and comparatively unknown for so able a minister ;—well be- loved and peculiar dear to his mother, who was the light and joy of her home and the stay and helper of her husband, when he shrank from the difficulties against which their ministers were called to struggle some 30 years ago, he seemed to inherit his father's gentleness and mother's alluring influence and fervent affection. In the struggles of a family of many children and with limited means, he early manifested the unselfish and generous spirit which was one of the main characteristics of his life, and how his father con- sulted with him and trusted even to leaning upon him in very early life be (the speaker) knew full well ; while the mother's eye kindled and her fact was radiant as she told of the gem-like qualities of her eldest boy. His conversion strikingly illustrated the consistency of his parent's home life. He was converted under the ministrref his father. A few years after that gracious and happy event he engaged himself in a lucrative situation for a term of years. Then his lore of souls became glowing with a fervent heat and an impression of his call to the work of the ministry lay heavy en his heart. But there were several brothers reaching that age when provision must be made for them, and directions given as to their future. Then there Came an irreparable loss and sad bereavement—the mother he adored was stricken; and with little premonition died, and the father was so shat- tered by the stroke that he never recovered his former self. At this junctnre the son felt that whatever might be his fnture, it was his present duty to take his father's place and help his brothers into situations, and provide means for thier sustenance. This' he told him (Mr. Eglinton) soon after his mother's death, and this in every case he did. Then the bond that tied him to his employer became oppreseive, until his gifts became so ap- parent, and his success in preaching so manifest that his employer, convinced he was destined to the work and office of a minister, generously cancelled his obligations. lie offered himself for such service, on with recommendation of the Kirkgate circuit, Bradford, to the district meeting held in May, 1873, and was accepted. An extract from the char- acter as drawn by the superintendent minister at that meet- ing might not be unacceptable. "For three years.he has been a local preacher," he says, "and has been very accept- able in this important service. The virtue of his preaching in the conversion of souls is unquestionable; his gifts, toe, are good; and having considerable advantages in education, utterance, and manner, he promises to be an attractive as well as a useful preacher. At the quarterly meeting he passed unanimously and cordially, and he offers himself for the home work. (Signed) Joseph Heaton." How much and how soon he fulfilled the promise indicated in the fore- going extract his subsequent though short career gave grow- ing evidence. Accepted by the conference of 1873, he was sent to Ileadingly College, Leeds, where, although his etey was short, he most favourably impressed his fellow students, one of whom the Rev. John Foster, the missionary at Florence, who had hoped to welcome him to his house wrote that gentleness and deep spirituality were his characteristics while at Headingly, and that daring his college life he never heard an unkind word said by him or of him. Be had not, howevcr. been long at college before he was sum- moned to the death bed of hit father, and after his decease was directed by the rreeident of the Conference to labour in the circuit bereaved by his death. Gladly would the churches there have further retaintd his valued services, but connexional law and requirements constrained his removal at the next conference, by which he was appointed to Brigg, ,in Li.ncolnshire, where be remalead two years, the obliga- tions of the circuit at the cenclusion not pertnittine, a longer residence of ail unmarried minister. Of his great accept. end muss while there he (the preacher) was happily observant, being stationed in Lincoln at the same time, and the people were delighted to welcome him to officiate in the spacious chapels of that city. From Brigg he removal to the large and important Louth circuit, to which - he was invited and where hie fame as a- preacher and eloquent platform speaker had preceded him. Hero he attracted very large congregations to the spacious and commodious chapels. whose history was associated with the names of several of their most distinguished ministers and most eventful times. Hither he brought as a happy bride, full of joy and hope, the disconsolate and all but heart-broken widow who now so deeply mourned his removal; and here it was that under the strain of mental and physical exertions his health gave way. At that time he was exceedingly popular,and great demands were made upon his strength; and el though he declined many invitations for extra parochial service, he could not forbear sometimes to yield to the earnest solicitation of friends who neededltis help ; and so in various circuits be charmed and edified by his by hie attractive style and earnest address, his evangelical ant powerful preaching, the crowds who gathered to bear him. They knew how elegant and chaste was his diction, I the charm and grace of his elocution and his vivid Illustrations, and shove all, his spiritual fervour, as lie preached the Word whose power he felt and the Divine Redeemer he supremely loved. The Rev. 11. R. Burton, wrote tolim (Mr. Eglinton) as follows I was much troubled to hear of the death of my late much esteemed colleague the Rev. F. S. Hagen. As his superintendent the colleague, last two years of his active ministry I was very closely associated with him. I soon learned to respect him for his rare qualities of mind and heart, and as the result of more perfect acquaintance with him I esteemed and loved him for excellences he possessed, and which only a close iinimacy revealed. Naturally be was reserved, and sometimes when with his friends or in mixed companies lie would be so reticient that perhaps he might not draw a 'stranger to him. Then on other occasions he would manifest such a manly independence, or even resent what he deemed to be mean or wrong as might make some sore under his quiet though merited rebuke. He was, however, uniformly kind and petite. I never knew him do a mean thing or act iu , any way unbecoming his vocation as an ambassador for Christ.- His courtesy and open-handed generosity to the poor won him their love and blessing. As a colleague he was true hearted and unassuming, though popular. As a minister he set before him the high standard of excellence which he desired to reach in all his discourse, and he laboured hard to get the best thoughts and illustrations for all his sermons and addresses." Long before his three years had expired at Loath the best circuits of the neighbourhood desired to engage him for the next year. His earnest wish, however, to serve his Warrington Meads as well as possible had led them on his recommendation to engage him as their junior minister. Duriog tbe spring of 1879 hi health began to fail, his colleagues relieved him all they could, and all fondly hoped that with returning fine weather and God's blessing, or a change, he might recover his wonted eigour. His feebleness, however, increased, and his medical atten- dant appalled his friends by the serious view he took of the lease. When he, with Mrs. Hagen, came to his study to tell him the doctor's view, his feelings overpowered him, and in his feebleness and sorrow he could only weep. From his dear wife he had to learn his real condition, and at once arranged to relieve him from all work. After some weeks he appeared much better, and as his skilful medical man ex- pressed a decided opinion that he would be equal to a quiet country circuit, he endeavoured to carry out the suggestion. div.head: LATEST NEWS.
div.p: LATEST NEWS.
THE MISSING BALLOON:,

The Central News states-the belief is now generally gaining ground that the missing balloon must have dropped in the Channel, a few miles south of Bridport. This decision has been arrived at from the fact that a deal of gas, I some ten -thousand feet at least, had been permitted to escape from' the Saladin before Mr. Gardner and Captain Templer left the car, and that when last seen Mr. Powell was standing tm in the basket grasping the valve line. The probability, is that he intentively laid had of the line when it was torn from Captain Templer's grasp, and pulled the rope in order to bring the balloon down as near as possible. Mr. Powell no doubt reckoned upon an immediate pursuit after the balloon, and he may have hoped to maintain him- self afloat in the water until reached by some craft. The theories that be may have bean carried any great distance arc no •: generally disregarded, especially in oMcial circles, and it is thought that should the balloon be even speedily recovered the chances are that Mr. Powell's body has long before this been washed out of the car.

div.head: [I3IIIDPORT TELEGRAM LAST NIGHT.]
div.p: [I3IIIDPORT TELEGRAM LAST NIGHT.]

No news of the missing ballon has been received here irp to to-night, but everything that tan be done is done. Re- pated commuoications pass between Brixham, Alderney* London, and Miss Cosen's head office, Weymouth, but no success has been reported as having attended the search Of IL M. S. Dasher, and the several fishing vessels which were sent from Alderney, Cherbourg, atd other places. Captain Templer expresses the opinion that it would have been tan- possible for any Papansia,n of gas to have suffocated Mr. Powell on the balloon ascending as suggested.

div.head: WARRINGTON INFECTIOUS DISEASES HOSPITAL AND OUT•DOOR PAUPERS. *
div.p: WARRINGTON INFECTIOUS DISEASES HOSPITAL AND OUT•DOOR PAUPERS. *

The following question and answer appeared in the last issue of the Local Government Chronicle, which will be interesting to the ratepayers of Warrington:— "Deputy Town Clerk" writes:—" Will you kindly give rnd your opinion upon the points raised in the following case :—The Corporation of this borough have extensive powers under a local act for the compulsory notification of infectious diseases, and the removal of persons suffering therefrom to a hospital belonging to the Corporation. In the exercise of these powers during an epidemic of scarlet fever, which has rec.n:ly prevailed in the town, several cases of fever amongst out-door paupers have come under our notice which we have not interfered with, the Corporation having refused by resolution to receive pauper patients into the hospital. We contend that it is the duty of the board of guardians to provide hospital accommodation for their patients, whether they be in-door or out-door paupers; upon this point, however; there seems to be a diversity of opinion. Glen, in his 9th edition of the Law of Public Health, p. 125,. rays: ' Th 3 (Public Health) Act makes no distinction between pauper and non-pauper cases, and it is therefore equally incumbent upon an urban authority on whom the statute has imposed the duty of taking precautions against the spread of infectious disertass to provide hospital accom- modation for the isolation of persons of all classes so in- fected; whilst, on the other. bend. Lumley, in his work, p. 108, notes that the word ' inhabitants' (for whom by sec. 131 it is incumbent upon urban authorities to provide) 'does not apply properly to paupers who are to be provided for by the board of guardians.' I may point out that Glen further gives, on page 125, a form of agreement between an urban authority and a board of guardians for the reception of paupers into a hospital belonging to the former body. You will observe that in sec. 25 of the copy sections of our local Act (herewith enclosed) that upon the certificate of the medical officer . . . . that any person within the borough is suffering, &c., the Corporation may exercise their powers. It is contended by the guardians that this applies to their out-door paupers, because they are persons residing within the borough; and, further, that as they pay rata; ithough , these are compounded for by the owner and only indirectly, I paid, if at all, by the tenant in the way of rent), they are- . I within the legal definition of 'ratepayers,' and entitled to all ; the benefits given by our Act; they also contend that the Public Health Act casts upon us the duty of Droviding for them. The guardians admit that it is their duty to provide hospital accommodation for their in-door paupeis, and that if the out-door paupers come in the house, they would then of course be provided for; but does it follow that because the guardians, for their own convenience, or because they have not room in the" house for all their paupere, permit them to stay out, the urban authority mast provide for them in case of sickness ? The broad question is, who is bound lb , provide hospital accommodation for out-door paupers ?" Anstcer.—lt appears to us that when the removal to a hos- pital of a person suffering from an infectious disease is necessary for the isolation of the patient, and not in con- sequence of his destitution, the case should be provided for by the sanitary authority. The fact that the sanitary authority have provided a hospital for infectious cases does not, in our opinson, relieve the guardians of the obligation to afford the relief which is requisite in the case of any destitute person suffering from infectious disease. Any , relief which may be required in such a case, including I medical attendance, nursing, &e, should, as it appears to us, Ibe given by the guardians; and when, for the purpose of ' relief' removal to a hospital is necessary, the requisite pro- vision should be made by them. When a hospital has been ' provided by the sanitary authority of the district, it is I usually found convenient for the guardians to enter into an 1 arrangement with the sanitary authority for the admission i into the hospital of pauper cases, on terms agreed upon by , the two authorities.

The spec- tacle is strange of a successful trader thus trying to kick down the very ladder by which he has risen; but we do find men singularlY wrong-headed and reactionary in these respects. _Another able speech by Mr. 3. K. Cross, the member for Bolton, spoken at Leigh, on ,Tuesday evening, goes fully into the commercial bearings, of this question of Free Trade against retaliatory Protection ; and if Mr. Eoroyd really wants some hard nuts to crack, we would sug- gest that he had better make a meal upon this speech of Mr. Cross, before he clamours for mote victuals in the form of arguments in defence of Free Trade. In a short time, if trade keeps good, this agitation against a liberal tariff will probably die anatnral death; but in the meantime, the two or three mediocrities of the Tory Party who at present head it, would do well to display a little more modesty, and would not be so fond of posing as political wiseacres who undertake to instruct our veteran statesmen in the truths of poli- tical economy.,

I read the report of the lecture by the Rev. George Hack, at Camden Chapel, Runcorn, with a good deal of interest; and in it I found one statement which particularly attracted my attention. It was that at the recent Ecumenical Con- ference of Wesleyan Methodists, there were representatives of 24,000,000 members, including the offshoots of the body, —the largest Protestani.denotnination in the world. In the face of a statement like this, it is amusing, as showing the changes which the whirligig of time brings about, to take a peep at the works of the Rev. Sydney Smith, M.A., who once was residentiary canon:of St. Paul's, London, and edited the Edinburgh 'Unica before it fell• into the hands of Lord Jeffery. In revfEwing a book entitled "Strictures on two Critiques in the Edinburgh Review, on the subject of Methodism and. Missions," the fashionable preacher uses language which would have sounded far better if it had come from the mouth of a tavern brawler, instead of from one who Voressed Christianity. I give a few samples from the critique referred to, which I would remind my Noncon• form ist readers were written in 1809, and that the" reverend" critic only left this world about 1340. In speaking of "sober and rational Christianity," he says :—" We are quite ready; if any fair opportunity occur, to defend it, to the best ef our ability, from the tiger-spring of infidelity and we are quite determined if we can prevent rach an evil, that it shall not be eaten up by the 'tasty and numerous vermin of Methodism." Pro- ceeding, he says: "It is scarcely possible to reduce the drunken declamations of Methodism to a point, to grotsp the wriggling lubricity of these cunning animsls and to fix them in one position." He states that Methodishical in- structors pilfer the people of all their money, And then bring about the following dreadful results :—Tircy "shut them out from all their dances and country wakes," and they are afterwards "sent penniless into the fields, to gaze on the clouds, and smell to (sic) dandelions." Further on the "reverend" gentleman observes :—" Undoubtedly, the dis- tinction of mankind into godly and ungodly—if by godly is really meant those wile apply religion to the extinction of had passions—would be.highly desirable. But when by that word, is only intended a sect more desirous of possessing the appellation than of deserving it, when, under that term, are comprehended thousands of canting hypocrites and raving enthusiasts—men despicable from their ignorance, and for- midable from their madness—the distinction may hereafter prove to be truly terrrific • and a dynasty of fools may again sweep away both Church and State in one hideous I ruin." I will not quote any more of the ',Rev. Sydney's effort at criticism; but leave your readers to meditate on the courtesy with which Nonconformists were treated in this country some eighty years ago. When at times I have heard some member of the Legal Hundred talk with auch unction about the Established Church, and act the part of a flatterer to the Establish- ment, I have wished that there was a little more of true manhood and independence in him. The Wesleyan Methodist ministry.do not require patronage, but fair play and courtesy from their ministerial brethren of the Church of Engldnd. It may be said that quoting the rubbish I uttered by Sydney-Smith cannot do any good, but I con- sider that the reading of such sentences, may, possibly, I prevent too much coquetting with the Church of England by some Wesleyane, and may cause the clergy of that body to feel ashamed of the intolerance which sometimes marks the members of their order when dealing with those who claim a right to exercise their private judg- ment concerning those who in that embodiment of wisdom known as the catechism are described as "their pastors and mast era." The miners of this district will no doubt be glad to learn that the National Miners' Conference at Eirmingham! on Thursday, adopted a resolution in favour of the formation of a National Federation of Miners. There can be no doubt that organisation amongst this hard-working body of men ;has been the means of improving their legal and financial position, and if union is beneficial when 4t exists as at pres,nt, it would he far more beneficial if the whole of the miners throughout the kingdom were joined together in one grand federation. Mr. Thomas Burt, 11. P., has been elected president of the National Association of Miners, a position rendered vacant by the death of the late Mr. Macdonald, Mr. Burt not only commands the esteem of the miners generally but his manly and independent bearing and integrity hes won for him the respect of all classes of society. The discussion which took place at the Prescot Board of Guardians this week, relative to the relief of WOfliOfl whose husbands had gone away or are in prison, revealed a curious state of affairs in which the ratepayers must feel particularly interested. On reference to the remarks made by the Guar- dians, it will be seen that over £l5O had been expended in the St. Helens districts for the relief of families of this class, whilst at Prescot £l7 had been so spent, and at Widnes not one single penny ! I presume that in Widnes they order all these p mpl e into the house, and with all duo deference to the opinion expressed by Mr. Jackson that such a course would necessitate the enlargement of the Union, I venture to say that the course will be found as beneficial in the other dis- tricts as at Widnes. and that it would tend very materially to a reduction in the amount of relief now given to those who scheme to be a burdea on the ratepayers whenever and wherever they can.

div.head: 'EXAMINER, SATURDAY, DECEMBER 17, 1881.
div.p: THE 'EXAMINER, SATURDAY, DECEMBER 17, 1881.

On Monday 6vening, the ratepayers of Runcorn will be called upon to decide whether a Free Library shall be established in the town or not. Thanks to the efforts of those who have laboured to benefit the town in the past, the rates are very reasonable, compared with those paid by the people of Widnes. I feel confident from all that has been said on the subject, that it is not intebded to spend any great amount of money on establishing such a boon; and I hope that each ratepayer who is intavour of the scheme, will take care to take a companion with him to the meeting, in which case the requisite majority will easily be main'ained. Let those who-think the people of Runcorn would be bene- fited by such an institution not forget to be present at the meeting. There is an old saying that what is everybody's !mines is nobody's. If the lovers of books would have their pet project carried out, let them attend the gathering, and not trust to there being a sufficient number to carry it. There is not the slightest doubt that some of those who are sure to vote against the proposal, would not be so dull on some questions if they would develop their intellectual powers by reading. Strangers are not loved in Runcorn ; and if the inhabitants wish to keep whatever good things there are in the town in their own hands, they must give the rising generation a fair chance in the fight by seeing that they are as educated as men from other towns, and as capable of filling any good appointment which may happen to fall vacant. FLACCUS.

ITALTON PARISH CHURCH MITIDAL Istruovumnrr So- CIRTY.—The usual weekly meeting in connection with the above society was held on Tuesday evening last, when Mr. Tandy occupied the chair; and there was an excellent attendance of members. A paper entitled "The Policy of the present Government," was given by Mr. B. Haddock, at the conclusion of which there was a lively discussion. FORBIDDING THE Beres.—There was considerable excitement in SL John's Church, Farnworth, on Sunday. The vicar was publishing for the third time the banns of marriage between John Dunn and Margaret Robinson, when an elderly man rose from the body of the church and ex- claimed, "I forbid those banns." Ile was requested to enter the vestry at the close of the service, and he then stated that-the intended bride was his daughter, and that she was only 14 years of age. Of course, such an objection is fatal to the marriage.

WAILVINGTON Imgramart.—The secretary aelm-ow- ledges with thanks the sum of £29 61. Sd.. received from the Workingmen's Committee to promote subscriptions to this Institution, being the net proceeds received at their success- ful concert last Saturday.

_ BEWSET Drama non ca. Horz.—An entertain- ment in connection with this Band of Hope was given on Thursday evening, in the Workmen's Club Hall. There was a good attendance. Mr. R. A. Naylor presided. The pro- gramme consisted of songs, recitations, Sze., from members of the following Bands of Ilepe :—B uttermatket-street and Penketh (Wesleyan) ; Brick-street, Friar's-green, Buckley. street, Wycliffe, Golhorne-street kliaptist) ; Howley (Unsec- tartan) ; and Workingmen's Mission, Bank Quay.

SANKEY BRIDGES WESLEYAN CHAPEL. - Mr. Elijah Ferd delivered his populav lecture on "Advice gratis, or taking care of number one," on Saturday. The lecture is got up in an ingenious style, making use of the letters of the alphabet for separate stibjects, and presented important lessons upon each subject. Votes of thanks to the lecturer, and to Mt. Collier for presiding, brought the meeting to a close.

LOST IN 7HB FOG AND DROWNED AT ItIINCOnN.—On Sunday, about 12 o'clock WON the body of a man, named Michael Calligao, who was abaut 40 years of age, was found in the Mersey at Runcorn. The deceased had not been seen since about, six o'clock on Saturday night, when be was drinking at the Boat House Inn, in Mersey-street. It is sup- posed that while under the influence of drink and confused by the thick fog that prevailed, he lost his way in going home, and walked into the river and was drowned. Mr. J. E. Worsley held an inquest at the Boat House Inn, on Monday afternoon. The jury returned a verdict of "Found drowned."

CONCERT IN AID OF LOCAL CHARITIES.—We would (gale the attention of our readers to the opportunity offered on Monday evening next, of listening to a good concert for a praiseworthy object. We understand that the proceeds, after payment of expenses, are to be handed over to the Committe of old Men and Women's Christmas Treat Fund. The name of Madame Edith Wynne is, we believe, in itself sufficient to attract the attention of concert goers, while that of. Mr. Frank Weston, as a violoncellist, assures the lovers ot instrumental solos of a treat. The nature of his reception in the Public Hall on a very recent occasion leaves little doubt that he is a favourite with Warrington audiences. In addition to these attractions' the efforts of several well- known amateur vocalists will be directed towards providing a pleasant evening. From the list of pieces to be performed, announced in the advertisement on our front page, it will be seen that some new songs as well as a number of old favourites will be given. We trust that the attendance will be such as to permit of a respectable sum being realised for the purpose for which the concert is being given. WAPPTEGTON LADIES' SCHOOL OF INDLISTRY.—This school, which was established in 1814, was examined for the first time by one of Her Majesty's Inspectors last October, and Mr. Beamont, who takes a very great interest in the institution, tfas just received the report of the inspector from the Education Department. The following extract is taken from the report :—This, the oldest school but one of the elementary schools in Warrington, has been reorganised tend r a scheme of the Endowed Schools Commissioners,and now for the first time claims annual grants. The main room is fairly suitable, but the class rooms besides being down- stairs, and impossible to be constantly supervised by the head teacher, are in themselves unsuitable. I am glad to learn that steps are at once to be taken to provide a good room for the first standard, where I hope an adult teacher will be placed. The mistress is most zealous, and considering the short time for preparation, the increase in the numbers, and backwardness of the majority of the children, there has been done a good and promising work. The Children have passed a satisfactory examination, and are in very fair order. Kate C. Cleveland and Esther M. J. Morgan have passed

LECTURE ON " PB.ESIDENT GARFIELD " AT RUNCORN. -The Rev. J. J. Jones, of Runcorn, on the night of the 9th inst., at St. John's Chapel, Runcorn, gave a lecture founded on the life of President Garfield. The lecturer is the author of the temperance tale "Slain by drink." The lecturer minutely described the life of the late President, touching upon the principal events which have made his name a household word over the civilized world. SERVICE or BONG AT Wnsmose. - The choir of Weston Point Wesleyan Chapel on the night of the 9th inst. gave a service of song, entitled "Her Benny." The service was given at the Wesleyan Day School, and there was a good attendance. The story of "Her Benny" is adapted to some very excellent music, aod sustains a pathetic interest throughout. The choir rendered the piece with much ex- pression. Mr. R. Norman was in the chair, and the connec- tive readings were given by Mr. L. Rosenberg. ALLEGED THEFT OP HOUSE...MOLD EFFECTS.- At the. Runcorn 'Police Court, on Wednesday last, before Mr. James Reynolds, a woman, 'named Margaret Cooke, who is under Police supervision, yes chaled with having, on the 10th December, stolen a dolly, three mugs, two saucepans, a bucket, and two tables, the property of Sarh Ann Allaby.-The parties live near each other in Mersey-street, and the identity of the stolen property having been proved, it was given in evidence that the prisoner had sold the things to a woman named Jane Drury.-Sergeant McMichael apprehended the prisoner, but she denied all knowledge of the articles.-There was another charge against the prisoner of having stolen a saucepan, the property of Jane Caholane-It was proved that the sauce- pan was missing from the house of the prosecutrix, and that it was subsequently found at the house of the prisoner.- She was committed for trial at Knutsfotd Sessions on both charges. DEATII OF MR. CAIERYTTItEES, or EfALTON.-01IT Runcorn readers will deeply regret to hear of the death of Mr. William Carruthers, surgeon, of Halton, which took place on Monday afternooq, at the age of 72 yeara. De- ceased was most desei vedly esteemed, not only by the general public, but by the members of his profession. He took cold on the previous Wednesday, and never afterwards rallied. He came to Bellcore about forty years ago, and commenced a practice, which rapidly became an extensive one. He afterwards went to Halton where he continued to practice. He was a member of the Royal College of Surgeons, and his ability was so highly rated that be was in great request as a consulting surgeon. The bOdy of deceased was conveyed to its last resting place at Carlisle, there to be in- terred with the remains of his wife, on Thursday. Every house in the village had the blinds drawn to mark the respect in which the deceased gentleman was held. The hearse was followed by aeout fifty Oddfelloos, and there were several private carriages containing relatives and friends of the deceased. Runoller EA.EISU QM= CEOIR.-A few days ago several members of the Runcorn Parish Church choir pre- vailed upon Mr. Johnson, the organist, to obtain a " pass " from Messrs. Inman and Co., Liverpool, to enable them to look through their magnificent steamer, "City of Rome,' on Saturday last, which was then lying in No. 2 Branch Alexandra Dock. Owing te the dense fog whiCh prevailed only eight Or tea laetaons out of 21 turned up at the station ' at 1-35 p.m., but the were not to be deterred from under- taking a perilous railway journey. As is customary in foggy weather, the train in which they traveled arrived a few minutes toe late at Edge Hill for them to catch the Bootle train, and they had in consequence to proceed to Lime-street. They next walked to the Exchange, and took a 'bus to the north end. The officers on board the steamer j had apparently been advised by Messrs. Inman and Co. of the intended visit, and they very kindly showed the party through the different saloons, &c., which were most elabor- ately fitted up. By the time these had been seen it was getting dark, and the company subsequently repaired to the well known rooms of Messrs. Fiske and Fairhurst, South Castle-street, and partook of a splendid tea, given by Mr. Whittaker. The rest of the evening was most agreeably spent in visiting the various places of amusement. TEE LATE Mae. ACTON, OF NORTON.-The funeral of Mrs. Acton, widow of Mr. John Acton, of Eanley Wood Farm, Norton, took place on 9th inst. The intelligence of the death of the lady was received with regret by a large circle' of friends in the neighbourhood of Norton Halton, and -Runcorn. She was the oldest tenant of Sir Norton, Brooke, Bart.. and the family have held Emilei Wood for three suc- cessive generations. The first part of the !melee service was conducted at Halton Parish Church, where the deceased was a regular attendant, by the Rev. John Lockwood. A psalm was chanted by the choir, and a hymm sung. CATEOLIC ENTERTAINMENT AT APPLETON.—The third of the series of entertainments which are being held daring the present winter on behalf of the proposed extension of St. Bede's Day Schools, took place on Thursday evening. The programme was a varied one, though the talent engaged was perhaps scarcely equal to that secured at the previous entertainments. The principal items in the programme were two dramatic pieces—a scene from "Who's to inherit." and one from " Gertrude's Money Box," in which Misses M. Lea, Julia 4nnersley, Canavan, Kavanagh, and others, took part. Popular songs and recitations made up the rest of the programme. '

BOY DIIOWNED AT WIDNES.—A drowning fatality °c- coned at Widnes on Wednesday morning. The victim was named Thomas Edward Jenkins, 11 years of age, residing with his parents in Leigh-street, Lugsdale. He attended the Warrington-road Board School, and on Wednesday morning left borne about half-past eight o'clock, intending to go to school. When he got near tho school his attention was arrested by the fact that the large pit in the field hard by was frozen over, and the firm, smooth appearance of the ice tempted him to venture on it. At first the ice seemed able to bear his weight:, but when be got into the centre it cracked and yielded beneath him, and he was at once sub- merged. A man named Neale witnessed the accident, and fetched P.C. Strickland to the spot. Grappling irons were obtained, and fresh assistance soon arrived; but it was quite an hour before Jenkins could be got out of the water, and be was then quite dead.

Dist:tors= AT Hitrzwoon.—A minus discovery was made at Macket's House farm, situated on Lord Derby's estate at Halewood, a few days ago. Some workmen were engaged in taking down a wall in the honse against which there had been a cupboard, when to their surprise they found an inner cupboard let in in the thickness of the wall. It was aboht a foot square, and of the same height as the adjoining room. There was a door to it, secures( by a pad- lock. The whole was only screened from observition by a thin coating of plaster. The man engaged in the work at once broke open the door, but the mysterious cupboard, which, according to all preconceived notions on the subject, should have been the hiding place of some miser's hoard, or secret of the past, was disappointingly empty. The house is about a hundred years old, and has been in the occupation of its present tenants for 59 years. Th mgh the outer cup- board had been in consistent use during that period, the ex- istence of the hidden cupboard was never suspected. At a meeting held in Chester, on Saturday, it Was resolved to form a Dairy Farmers' Association for the county, one object being to secure the holding of monthly cheeee fairs in this city. RELIGIOUS CENSUS AT NANTWION.—A. census has been taken of the attendance at public worship in Nantwich on a Sunday recently, with the following result: At morning service, 1,759; evening, 2,421. The population is 7,450. There are eleven places of worship in the town. The Wes- leyan chapel heads the list with a total morning and evening attenclance of 1,275; the pariah church being next via, 1,286. 000/tllKbaz letiSSiOtT MUTUAL IMPROVILISENT SOCIEIt, —The seventh meeting of the session was held on Monday night in the Mission Room, when. Mr. Musket gave an essay on "Tobacco." The essayist gave medical proof that tobacco is poisonous and injurious to the human system, and that it led many young men to drink. After some dis- cussion had taken place, the essay was approved, and several members pledged themselves to abstaiu from the use of tobacco. ZYALOTIC DISEASE, ITS DETECTION EY a CIIMITTNG."—II has often been felt by Sanitary Reformers and others in- terested in the public health that the present system of re- porting zytnotic disease to local authorities by their medical officers, is in many respects faulty. What is wanted is the localisation of cases of illness (or death) and an accurate continuing record for fature reference. This has at last been supplied, the inventor of the system being Mr. W. W. Yates, of Dewsbury (formerly connected with a Warrington journal now extinct.) The scheme which it may be stated leas just been submitted ta, and favourably received by tho Medical Department of the Local Government Board,—is that each local autherity should have an outline mapbt its district prepared in sections, and Ova cheap copies should be supplied to the medical officer. Co these he would, month by montb, mark in coloured ink the exact spot where death, (or illness', occurred through any of the chief zystatic diseases. For instance red for smalatina ; black, enteric fever ; pink, small pone light blue, emulates •' chrome, diarrtce ; pionna, whooping coagh ; and green, diphtheria and croup. By retaining 'these charts, se marked, disease-prerlucing areas would manifest themselves uumistakeably, Ffral then the cause could all the more readily be ascertained and re- moved.

THE "ZULU WAR" AVEILS3LSTON'S CIRCUS.—Th,3 representation of the leading incidents in the war in-Zulu- land has keen the chief feature of the performance at Harmston's Circus this week. The spectacle has been pro- duced on as extensive a scale as the arena will admit of, and the representation was such as to maintain the interest of the audience throughout. The Zalu war dance was admirably Performed by Cetewayo's fullowers, and the battles of Isandula and Ulundi were reproduced in a most graphic manner. An impressive scene was the battlefield by moon- light; while the enthusiasm of the onlookers was provoked by the realism of Lieut. Melville's exciting fight to save the colours. The performance concluded with an effective tableau—the capture of Cetewayo. The principal parts were taken by members of Mr. Harmston's capital company, and it only remains to be said that all acquitted themselves ad- mirably, the ludicrous adventures of Pat Murphy (Mr. Bell), the war correspondent, being much enjoyed. Mons. Leander performed some really clever balancing feats, and the risible faculties of the audience were greatly exercised by the eccentric and witty clowns, Messrs. Cruickshank, Armstrong, and Lemaire; while the acrobatic performances of the Transfield Troupe; and the equestrian e2hibitions by Madame Gaertner, Madame Caroline, Mr. Yelding, and jklaster P, Ihirmston, added much to the evening's enjoy-

After tea Mr. Matthew Bowden presided, and called upon Mr. J. Ungar& as the oldest member of the committee, to present to Mr. Wm. Reberts a handsomely bound edition of the Revised Testament similar to those recently presented to the Mayor and Mayoress. Mr. Lingard, in a few well chosen words, congratulated Mr. Roberts upon the success of his work, and asked-him to accept the present, which had been so unanimously agreed to by the committed. Mr. Roberts thanked the committee for their handsome gift. It was altogether unexpected, because be had felt that in being selected by ,a unanimous vote to act as secretary to the centenary, that in itself was the greatest honour which could have been offered him. He had done his best to make that .centenary celebration worthy of the Nonconformist schools of Warrington, and should ever -cherish in his memory a happy recollectien of that magnificent g tthering of 5,000 Sunday school teachers and scholars in front of the Town Hall, in August 1850. He should prize that book net only in affectionate remembrance of the donors but also because of the generous sentiments which hai,been ex- pressed in acknowledgement of his efforts to promote unity and mutual good feeling amongst the various schools. The Testaments were afterwards handed over to the - various schools. Votes of thanks were accorded to the chairman and the treasurer. Mr. John Hall, for their services.

GLASS BLOWING IN AMERICA. Sir wishyou would allow nee a short space in your valuable paper to warn my coantrymen against the reports that are sent to England concerning the high wages that are made in this country by glassblowers, which in 19 cases out et every 20 are false. The facts are as follows :—There are men come here expecting to make five or six dollars a day, but in most of the cases it is one or two dollars a day, and worse still not half of them get any employment, as the country is over-supplied with glassblowers ; but the employers want to over run the country with men, as they are determined to reduce the wages of those who are employed. I have only been a short time here, but I have seen some distressing cases of men who I know left good situations at home and came here, but could not get a day's work. We have seven spare bands here; some get a day's work and others none. It is the same at a great many more factories—a surplus ofilabour. I would strongly advise ray fellow tradesmen to be very cautious about the advertise- ments mad the promises'the agents make when they want to engage them, as I have met men who were promised great wages when they landed here. It was all a farce and not -what the agents represented; but I would say to them not on any account come out at present. I will now conclude, Mr. Editor, hoping you will give this publication, and remain'' JOHN WILSON. 468, Market-street, Philadelphia.

FRIGHT AND FLIGHT OF JUVENILE CONSERVATIVES. Sir,—The Conservatives of the Warrington Parliamentary Debating Society have been fairly run to earth: the,helpless condition in which they were situated was obvious from the commencement of the present session; still, while there was ' life there was hope, and efforts were put forth to bring in recruits, but without any substantial results, and it became ominously apparent on each succeeding meeting that Con- servatism had no boll upon the intelligent youth of our sow Radical borough. Two Liberal innings and one Con- servative innings has sufficed to put to flight the buds of Cerservatism in Warrington. The leader of that party, no doubt, has all along felt his forces were inadequate to con- tend against the unflinching Liberal opponent. His two aides-de-camp, no doubt, did their best to support and en- courage him to stand his ground; but all to no purpose, the sniserable rank and file could only cheer or sneer as occasion served. I beg pardon, they could give a solid vote on any question, according to the dictates of their leader. Discus- sion appeared to he a word they had not found in their vocabulary; and, consequently, were ignorant of its mean- ing, thus rendering them helpless in the face of the enemy. They appear to be in the position of a family just entering upon life's stage whose parents had neglected to educate them, and therefore were totally unprepared for life's work. The leader, realising his weak position,took the first favourable opportunity to abandon it, anci, like the great trickster, whom he so much admire], made use of the speech of the member for Northampton as a pretext to cover his retreat Into—let us hope—oblivion. But never was a pretext more hollow or transparent : the sham was apparent to all who witnessed the scene, and are acquainted with subsequent events. All true citizens must regret that such an educa- tional institution as the Parliamentary Debating Society has come to grief, for had the Conservatives persevered another yearperhaps they tright have had such acquisitions to their thinned ranks as would have enabled them to stand their ground creditably; as it is, the inference to be drawn from their collapse cannot be otherwise than that they are in a hopeless minority; and if that be so, then Radical Warring- ton has nothing to fear for a long time to como.—Yours, ANTI-SHAM.
THE CLOSING OF SUNDAY AND DAY SCHOOLS AT

NEWTON. Sir,—Will you Madly insert the following correspondence which came before the teachers of the Congregational school, on Sunday last, as many enquiries have been made as to whether the Sunday as well as the day schools were to be closed for a tnontb ?—Yours respectfully, P. M. CAMPBELL. etvton, 12li Dee, 1881.—Superintendent Congregational School, Newton-le-Willows. Nen ten-in-INlalterfield Improvement Commissioners.-2, Calro•street, Warrington, 7th December, 18S1—Der Sir,—l urm directed bythe Commissioners to inform you that at a con- ference of commissioners and school mmagers of this dis- trict, held on Monday last, it was unanimously resolved to I close the Sunday and day schools of this district for three weeks from the 16th instant. As your school was not repre- canted at the conference, I am directed to request your co- operation in this endeavour to diminish the spread of, infections disease in the district.—! am, sir, yours truly (signed) Jamss E. WORSLEY.—Rev. .1. Allatt, crow- lane, Newton.le-Willows. The Manse, Newton-le-Willows, Lancashire, 9th December, I 1881.—Dear Sir,—l have to acknowledge receipt of your favour of the 7th inst. stating that at a conference of com- missioners and school managers of this district, held on, Monday last, it was unatimonsly resolved to close the Sun- day and day schools of the district from the 16th instant, and raj:testing our co-operation. On inquiry I find that no information respecting the meeting referred to was given to any one connected with the Congregational schools here, or those schools would have been represented. I will under- take to place your letter before my friends on Sunday next, and I tkink I may promise that we shall be prepared to act in harmony with other schools in the district in the matter referred to. It is a disadvantige that we know nothing of the facts presented to the conference, and have not therefore the same means of forming a judgment as those who took part in it. I find that there is unanimity as to the closing of the day schools. We have no day school, and hence are not concerned with that question. NI ith regard to the Sunday schools, however, I find no disposition to close. The managers of some of the Sunday schools knew nothing whatever of the proposal until they heard it from me in the course of my inquiries.—l am, dear sir, yours truly (signed), JAME 9 ALLATI —To James E. Worsley, Erq. Newton-in-Makerfield Improvement Commissioners.-2, Cairo•street, Warrington, 10th Dec., 1881.—Dear Sir,—I beg to thank you for your letter of yesterday's date, which I will lay before the commissioners. At the time Mr. Brierley sent out the notices proposing the conference it was only in- tended to suggest the closing of the day schools of the dis- trict. This will explain the cause of your not receiving a notice. At the conference it was thought desirable to close the Sunday schools also, and I was then instructed to write to yourself and to others upon the subject. lam very sorry that you were not present at the conference. The subject then discussed is, in the opinion of the .commissioners, a most important one, as their medical officer gives a most dccided opinion as to the desirability of keeping the'chil- dren of the district as much apart from one another as pes- t-le for an interval. There can be no doubt that it would e been much better if the conference had by the atten- dance of the managers of all the schools been able to come to a. definite decision as to a united course of action after the advantage derived from the fullest possible discussion of the subject.—l am, dear sir, yours truly (signed), JAMES E. WORALEY.—Rev. James Allatt.

Ea OF THE ORDER. which was well attended, tional School room, "OEnEhlCHondOaNy eTverinEingl,DaVmAlleectTinolGgr, deadn.d ad- vantages se of hearing an address from Mr. Temperance, for the purpose wßasunchorelnd, nindetrhethßee athuespadaices of the Order of the Sons of rchnestoerm, aosn sthtoer-mprai:cpiprelests vantages of the Malcolm Macleod,do_f The Cumumanr, in opening the proceedings, expressed the pleasure he felt at seeing such a good audience, which I clearly cause- proved to him that the interest in the temperance was not on the wane, but increasing year by year. Personally', he was of opinion that every man, woman, and ' child in the kingdom would be benefitted by becoming ab- stainers. If they only read their newspapers carefully, and noticed the terrible havoc drink was making in the world, it was enough to startle them. He believed that nine-tenths of the pauperism of the country, if it could be properly traced, would be found to be brought about by intemperance. Teetotalism had made rapid strides during the past few years; and the Christian denominations were now taking it up, which they ought to have done many years ago. Might, the day soon dawn when all should enrol themselves under the glorious banner of temperance. He urged all those who were parents to see to it that they trained their children not to touch drink, and if they did so, they might depend upon it that in the generations to come the mighty upas tree of intemperance would be destroyed, and the frightful misery which it caused blotted out from the face of the earth. Many of the pauper children in the workhouse at Ditton had been placed there owing to the intemperate habits of their parents. In the workhouse school they received a good education, and a moral training, and they were a thousand times better off than if they were growing up in the homes of drunkards where intemperance shed its baneful influence. The longer he lived, the more decided became hie convic- tion that every profeesor of religion ought to be an abstainer (hear, hear and applause), if from no higher motive, for the sake of example. In conclusion, he briefly directed the audience to consider the tremendous power of example, and I to remember that none of them lived unto himself, but Ills example exercised a power for good or ill. He hoped that they would have a capital meeting. (Loud applause). Mr Malcolm MACLEOD, who was received with applause, said he wished to warn the audience against expecting any grand bursts of eloquence which would almost fetch them off their seats, from him, as he was only a plain working man, who talked for the pleasure of doing so. His subject that night was not One which gave much scope to the imagination, it being, in effect, a sketch of the operations of the Sons of Temperance Society. They were all acquainted with the constitution of the secret orders, such as Oddfellows, Druids, and Gardeners, whose members had to pass the doctor, and, after being admitted to the lodges, contributed a small weekly sum for the pur- pose of providing in cases of sickness or death. The order of the Sons of Temperance was exactly on the same footing, as far as organisatidn was concerned, but left the lines upon which the other societies were established on the matter of intoxicating drinks, which they did permit their members to take. The result of this wise decision was that for every single member that died in their order, the other societies mentioned buried two. Therefore, they allowed the publi- cans to kill one half of their members! The Sons of Tem- perance promised their members lots of money if they died, but they would not allow them to die. (Laughter.) They were not a sick and burial society, whilst the others, just mentioned, were. They did net require to have any qualifi- cation to fain an ordinary friendly society, except that of good health, but to be a member of theirs they needed to have a back bone, in the shape of temperance principles, and to live up to them in the face of society. He would not waste a moment in supposing that there was any man present who would be content, when the time of sickness came, that his friends should support him, if by weekly contributions he could provide for the time of necessity. The system of insurance was so well understood in English society that it was not necessary even in a meeting of plain, working men, that he should spend one minute in explaining the principle of it. When a working man had made up his mind that hitnself, his family, and his children should not want for bread, when the time of sickness overtook him, his next duty was to select a society which could carry out the engagement it made with him. He should be able, in a very few moments, to show them that the .Sons of Temperance Society could do this, whilst many organisations were daily failing to do it, for the very reasons he had mentioned to them. Their society could not only pay money, but they could pay in for a longer period, and also save funds for the purpose of tiding over difficulties which overtook every society. They should also be anxious to join an organization the association with who3e members would not degrade them. Their society was finan- cially sound, and this was a vt ry important matter. In the lait number of their monthly journal—the Son'of Temperance—they had a return which had been made by two of the public accountants of London as to the largest district in connection with the Sons of Temperance Teey were all aware that friendly societies must have their assetts valued every year by some independent firm of ac- countants. The figures dealt with by the firm referred to in the case of the Sons of Temperance embraced 10,016 mem- bers of the order. -The computation showed that the rate of sickness attained a maximum in the middle period of life: • but, contrary to all expectation, the rate afterwards de- clined to a minimum. The accountants had drawn out a scale for the purpose of shelving what was the rate of sick- ness in this special society as compared with the rate amongst the Foresters and the Oddfellows. The result showed that from 18 to 21 years of age, the members belonging to the Order of the Sons of Temperance received about two days' pay per annum on account of sickness, and the Foresters six days. From the age of 36 to 64 there was scarcely any difference in the society's rate, and from 64 to 68 it was from one week each year down to scarcely a day for each member. They must mark that this applied to a very critical part of life, when the general vital statis- tics of the country clearly showed that sickness increased This showed that if a man lived a sober and virtuous life whilst he was young, Ile reaped the reward of so doing in old age by experiencing health. From 60 to 70 the returns showed scarcely a day's sickness. Such figures as these brought to his mind very vividly the passage in the Scriptures which said, " The wages of sin is death." The returns as to the societies in which drinking was allowed, showed that at the age of 59, reckoning from 44, they reached the rate of three weeks per annul-I'7l's sickness each member. At the age of 64, the Foresters' Society reached each year nine weeks' sickness, and the Oddfellows' eight weeks, and their rates continued to rise up to the end of life. He thoug,ht that a more striking instance of the beneficial results of total abstinence from intoxicating liquors could not be laid before an audience. However, in quoting the figures, he wished it to be clearly understood that he had no personal feeling against the excellent societies which he bad men- tioned, as they were in the highest degree beneficial to those who- would not go the length of becoming abstainers. The result of the calculations showed that the percentage of members sick in the Sons of Temperance was 132, and in the Foresters 298, or more than double. (Applause.) As to deaths, their society had 11.24 from 18 to 70 years of age and the Manchester Unity of Oddfellows, in the rural and city districte, 2084,- which was very nearly double. The Foresters bad 23, on more than double those of the Sons of Temperance. Some years ago he personally ex- amined the death‘rate throughout their whole order, and found it to be a little more than 8 per cent, per annum, whilst that of the friendly societies of the United Kingdom was 15.14, or nearly twice as many. • Their own order Wa, able to give its members more money for six months than the drinking orders could give them for three months. The latter discontinued the full payment at the end of three months, whilst the Sons of Temperance did not do so until the end of six months. The other orders dropped payment at the end of 12 months, but the Sons of Temperance continued to pay up to the and of sickness, it they were satisfied the clee was an honest one. (Applause.) If a man joined some of the friendly societies and he was bright, witty, intelligent, and his com- pany very acceptable, every one would put his glass before him, and the temptation to become a sot was strong in such a case. If a person was one of these selfish, hoggish fellows who could keep his thumb en a penny until he had put a mark upon It—(laughter)—he might go anywhere, for he would be safe, but in the case of a man who was open and generous hearted social company and the glass meant danger. He knew of a case in Manchester where a young man of splendid natural abilities had enabled him to "pass the chair " in one of these societies, but the social glass proved I is rain ;—the tie between him and his business was gradually snapped, and, to his knowledge, that young man ended his days in Salford workhouse! And this was far from being a solitary case. What was the difference when they joined the order of which he was a member.? 1 hey cttrtainly joined some very plain men, of whom it might be said that "they were none so good as they ought to be, and none so good as they could be,"—(laughter)—to slightly paraphrase a poetical couplet. There was not an angel among them—(laughter) ; but there was just this to con- sider—that if they took the worst one amongst them, they could not mend him with liquor. The sneaker next dwelt upon some of the silly slanders brought against abstainers; the fact that some of the highest physicians in the present day maintained that hlco- slatueinhnintfegdtewhotronogosemrvoslnntieleuydnp,uwfomrainotbnihnedtorhtuehedttehlfepelacomiitatnamb,ktoaehiumnuardg,t. hol u'as not good for the system ; and to the extremes of comoblnfeierielnnsi (Ito: autf aleotnarhi dnn. e apws preached cycedhhtsy:i chd, esael al ohivtdanegedreeyixhst aiuti delnlltl of Christ to roll away the stone at the grave of Lazarus, which to his mind proved very clearly that God would not' regenerate the universe by any miraculous act of interven- tion on His part, bet that all were responsible, in their individual capacity, for doing what they could to heal the "open sore of the world "—lntemperance. He concluded his address by an earnest appeal to those present to join in the labour of trying to sweep away the numerous liquor shops which filled our towns. During the evening the Weston band gave several nieces in good style; Mr. John Saunders a recitation, Mr. George Lacey a song the Misses Jones a duet, the Jones family a , song, and Messrs. Holt Brothers and T. Faulkner a recita- tion.
