SATURDAY.—Before Mr. Alderman Holmes. A DEsmarErt.—Dennis Clarke was charged with being an absentee from H.M. 52nd Regiment of Foot, stationed at Curragh Camp, Ireland, since the 2nd inst.—He was remanded to Walton to await an escort. ALLEGED THEFT BY A TAlLOR—Patrick Edwards, tailor, was charged on warrant with having, on the 26th October, feloniously stolen the sum of £6 6s, the property of Michael Gannon, Haydock-street.—Prisoner was remanded until Monday. Moamar.—Before the Mayor, Major Cartwright, and Councillor John Crosfield. A VIOLENT Dntrergann.---Alfred Jackson ,a young fellaw, was charged with being drunk and disorderly, and also with assaulting P.C. Taylor aud William Wheeler, who was assisting the farmer. He was also further charged with wilfully damaging the " snaps " to the extent of 2s 13d.— P.C. Taylor was on duty in Victoria-street on Saturday night, when he saw the prisoner in a house attempting to set fire to a window curtain. Afterwards he came out and went into a neighbour's house. Immediately there was a great noise, and the officer, on entering the house, saw the prisoner lying on the floor, bleeding very much from his face. Taylor brought him into the street, and prisoner at once " let loose " and kicked him in the mouth, legs, and stomach.—Wheeler said the prisoner was like a madman, and kicked him twice very severely.—Prisoner was fined 103 and cc)sts, and ordered to pay for the damage to the "snaps." HEARTLESS ROBBERY FROM AN EMPLOYER. THE FATAL POACHING AFFRAY IN
CHESHIRE.

PERCIVAL AND THE POACHERS COMMITTED. William Percival, farmer, was charged at the Altrincham Police Court, on Wednesday, with the marder of Joseph Jennings, and wit!r doing grievous bodily harm to James Perrin, tyro poachers at High Legh, on the 7th ultimo. Mr Marshall addressed the court for Percival, and said that the charge against the defendant was the most serious which could be made, and although it was not for them to I pronounce the final verdict as to whether the defendant was guilty or not, yet even if it was conceivable that they should commit him upon the most serious charge the result to him would be at any rate two months' agonising suspense ; prob thly his committahto gaol without bail, and an en- couragement given from the Bench to those bands of lawless men who went about the country poaching. They would have an encouragement to pursue their lawless course, and if Percival were committed for trial on the charge of wilful murder it would be direct encouragement to others in their position. Mr. Cobbelt, who conducted his case with his usual ability, had adopted the violent theory, which no impartial person could agree with—not that Percival fired the shot when in the heat of the affray, but that with a cold 1 bloodedness which one could hardly conceive he had delib- erately shot the man after the affray was over, anol when he was lying helplessly on the ground. The theory was extraordinary and evidently improbable, and was not borne out by the evidence. The evidence on the point was weak, and was not exhaustive, only three witnesses having been called, although there were upwards of a score who might have been. It had been suggested that Percival used his pistol in a most dastardly manner, but the evidence entirely failed to prove this. The poachers commenced the attack, after threatening the keepers, and if Percival fired in the course of the affray, the poachers being engaged in a felony and having fired upon him and his companions, who were, therefore, in danger he was perfectly justified in so doing. Lb e argued that the evidence entirely failed to prove that Percival had been guilty of the cold-blooded, the dastardly act of firing at Jennings, when be lay on the ground, to finish , Litin• Percival was justified in trying to arrest the poachers, who were committing a felony, and wilo had threatened tire keepers, and were carrying that threat into execution- If the Bench did not think that what had been done was justifiable, and they considered it their duty to commit hit, it would be for manslaughter, but under no circumstances whatever could he be guilty of the great crime of wilful murder. With regard to the second Fharge,Percival was in imminent peril, but if he shot Perrin in the lcgs he was justified in doing so. On the conclusion Of Mr. Marshall's address; the bench, after half-an-hour's deliberation, committed Percival for trial on the charge of nutuslanghter. Bail was granted in a total sum of £l,OOO. kr. Cohbett submitted that in the case of the poachers, Perrin, Ilitchin, and Willis, there was evidence for inquiry, and they were also committed for trial.
,IBERAL MEETING AT FRODSHAM.

ADDRESSES BY MR. PETER RYLANDS, M.P., AND MR. JAMES TOMKINSON. On Monday a crowded and enthusiastic meeting of West Cheshire electors was held in the Town Hall, Frodsham, under the presidency of Mr. Charles Reynolds. There were also present on the platform Mr. Peter Rylands, M.P., Mr. James Toinkinson, IP. (Liberal candidate for West Cheshire), Mr. John Simpson, Mr. F. Rigby, Mr. H. Linaker (Liberal agent), Mrs. C. Reynolds, Mrs. P. Rylands, and Mrs. Tomkinson. The CHArnstew, in his opening address, expressed his pleasure at haying again to be present at a political meeting in that town, and said that in holding such a meeting they were only following the example of other towns, for they found that over the length and breadth of the land the whole soul and heart of the people seemed to be thrown into the work of finding what information they could on the political subjects and en the stirring questions of the day. He must say that,from the 40 years during which there was no con- test in that division, they might think that this part of the world had more or less gone to sleep. Although the notice of this meeting was rather short, he thought they would not have found room for all the aspirants for political informa- tion. The last time be stood there the' were on the eve of the contest, when Mr. Tomkinson came forward as a candi- date for the division, and he put them in a first-rate position. It was not the most satisfactory result, as that would have been seeing Mr. Tomkinson at the head of the poll —(cheers)-- yet it was exceedingly satisfactory to everybody who had worked in his interest, and to those who were still ready to work for him, because they BO very largely reduced the majority against them on the former occasion. Now, be thought, after the result of the late registration, he might say with a considerable amount of confidence that they were quite ready to fight again—(cheers)—when they had the chance. He had no doubt the good work done at that re- gistration would show itself, and it would be found that, their first attempt having been a good one and their second a better, their next attempt would be better still, because they would he able to carry their man in. (Loud cheers.)

Mr. JAMES TOMICINSON, who was received with prolonged applause, said that since the last thus he addressed them in that hall many affairs, some important, had taken place; and lie was extremely glad to be able to come amongst them in order that they might interchange opinions, and see whether they Would favour him with their confidence at the next contest. (Hear, hear.) He felt that it was im- possible to bring anything new before them or throw any fresh light on subjects that had already been so thoroughly debated. At the same time he thought there had been so much misrepresentation on the other side, and such un- worthy motives imputed to the chiefs of the Liberal party, that it behoved everyone of them who wished well of his party to come before the electors of his division, and to rate as plainly as possible what he conceived to be the true state of affairs. (Cheers.) The range of public questions was so varied that it would be impossible for him to go over them all. He might carry them over Afghanistan or into Europe; but he thought the country had pretty well made up its mind that the Goveanment had done right both in their Asiatic and African policy. Whatever difference of opinion there might be they might truly say that they were at peace all over the world. In Europe there was profound peace, and he claimed for the present Government that it I was in a great measure due to the policy which it was car- rying du on the Continent. He should like to call their attention to matters more immediately interesting to them, inasmuch as they were nearer home. It would be affecta- tion to deny that the subject which at the present time occupied the minds of all was the question of Ireland. (Hear, hear.) Let them glance for a moment at Ireland's previous history. Without going back to the conquest of Ireland, and the narnerous confiscations, if they wont back only into the last century they would find that from time to time manufactures were started in the principal towns of Ireland. The unlimited water power , which was possessed gave them considerable advantage at a time when the power of steam was not known. As soon as Irish merchants began to compete with , the merchants of London, Bradford, Manchester, and other I English towns, so soon there went a deputation to the House of Commons representing that their industry was being in- terfered with by the Irish manufacturer, and begging that a prohibition should be put on. He was sorry to say that in every case that prohibition was at once granted. (Shame.) The result could only be one thing—that Irish manufac- turers were nipped in the bad, and the people were thrown for their:existenca and subsistence upon the soil; and so they had to the present day a population, with the ex- ception of a few towns in the north, dependent entirely upon the toil for their life and existence. There were till the year 1829 the most arbitrary, cruel, and unjust penal laws, by which anyone professing the Roman Catholic religion was subject to every sort of disability. They would, therefore, easily understand that the arbitrary removal of a man's holding meant exile and ruin, and any insecurity as to his tenure brought terror and disaffection. In 1870 Mr. Glad- stone made a great attempt to grapple with the difficulty. In Ulster a custom had grown up by which the tenant .had the right to sell his improvements on the land to another who would buy from him. The landlords of Ireland had not those improvements on the land which was done by English landlords. In a great Measure the improvements were done by the tenants, and there had grown up a system, to a cer- tain extent, of joint proprietorship in the soil. If a man had taken a farm, perhaps built his house, reclaimed the bog made roads, increased the value of his farm, he felt that to have his rent raised either to the full value or to be evicted was nothing less than spoliation and robbery. (Cheers.) In 1870, Mr. Gladstone made that into law which was only a custom. He made it illegal for a landlord te evict a tenant* as long as he paid him the rent. without paying him the value of the improvements, and a certain amount of com- pensation for the inconvenience and loss of all disturbances. It applied only to holdings up to £3O, because it was thought the larger tenants could take care of themselves. The land- lords complained, but within the next ten years the value of property in Ireland greatly increased. Then came bad seasons, and it was found that certain tenants were unable to pay their rents, and that some landlords were taking advantage of that fact to turn them out wholesale from their cottages, thereby confiscating their improvements and tenant right. Mr. Gladstone, in 1880, brought in the -Compensation for Disturbance Bill, which was a bill to prevent a bad landlord doing what no good landlord would do. (Cheers.) The Bill passed the House of Commons but it fared badly in the House of Lords, and was thrown out. A significant thing had been told him by Mr. Gladstone, that Mr. Parnell hild said in the lobby of the House of Commons to a member while the Bill was under discussion, that if it passed it would take the sting out of his agitation. Mr. Parnell had ulterior v:ews, and he (the speaker) did n..t think anything would have taken the sting out of the agitation. (Laughter.) The Land Act of 185 i was necessitated by the imperfect tneasure of success which followed the Land Act of 1870. In the debates in the House of Commons, and in the divisions, although certain Irish members abstained from voting at all, only one Irish member was found to vote against the Bill; and they should attach great importance to that fact. The Act secured to the tenant his property in the soil, and prevented the landlord from confiscating it. (Cheers.) There who no doubt that the past session was taken up by the Irish question, to the exclusion of many pressing Bills the Liberal Government wished to bring forward. It was disheartening to think of the small amount of work that had been got through by the Liberal party since they came into power. But no one would accuse them of idleness. The session of 1880 was remarkably trying. The members did not meet till the Ist May, but they sat till September, longer and later than any Parliament has sat for thirty years, in order to pass some Bills they thought were neces- sary. The Burials Bill was passed, and the Employers' Liability Bill. That was not a Bill intended to fine em- ployers, but to make them more careful of the lives and limbs of their servants. The Ground Game Act was opposed vigorously. The malt tax was taken off, and although the farmers and Conservatives had tried to do this for 30 years they now said it was worth nothing. (Laughter.) The first thing that was required to be done to enable the Government to pass such measures, which were needful for the good go- vernment of the country, was to amend the Parliamentary machine. They had seen the forms of Parliament misused, and such obstruction resulted as to practically cruse a block of business. It was, therefore, necessary that the obstruc- tion should he put an end to. He could not believe any right-minded man of either party would willingly lend him- self to oppose such a Bill to be brought in, by which the rights of mindrities would be respected, and at the same time with the sole object of repressing wilful andneedless obstruction. There was the qeeetion of the land laws. The land, owing to bad seasons, had attracted much attention, and rightly so, especially when they thought that the land was the staple trade of this country. They would see many of the obso- lete tr •mmels now surrounding the land struck off. The two.things that seemed to press were these—that there should be absolute security to the tenant for the im- provements he made to the farm, and the greatest encouragement to put his capital into it. (Hear, hear.) Another point was that the Law of Distress should be so modified as to put the landlord upon no worse or better footing than other creditors. The Conser- vatives brought in the Agricultural Holding's Bill, which was a good Act, to secure to the tenant tire value of the im- provements, but they put in a clause which made it optional with the landlord to say "I will, not be bound by it if I don't like." (Laughter.) All his own tenants were unner the Agricultural Holdings Act, and he had never had to sell one up, or nse the law of distress, and he hoped he never should have to do so. (Load cheers.) There was looming in the future the question of the extension of the fran- chise in the counties. (Cheers.) He must tell them what he thought would be good news, that, after working bard at the registration, they had calculated, and it was not on too sanguine a basis, that their gain on the total register of West Cheshire was 1,003 vote& (Cheers.) He believed that after making allowances for exaggeration, they had secured such a substantial majority as would carry the Liberal candidate at the head of the poll at the next election. (Loud cheers.) Mr. PETER RYLANDS, M.P., who was most heartily re- ceived, said allusion had been made to the fact that at the present time there was a good deal of Parliamentary, or extra-Parliamentary speaking. Statistics had recently been taken of the attendance at the various churches and chapels, and he was sorry to say that the number did not keep pace apparently with the increase of the population. But if they could have statistics as to the number of public meer Ingsoni political subjects, and the number of people attending ttih. en he believed they would And that they exceeded any nng which had been known before In the history of the kingdom.
He did not complain. He agreed with the chairman that it was a very gqpd thing to have political meetings. It .was very natural that there should be more, political. meetings
than used to be .the .case, and he woula tell . them why.

Thanks to the Liberal party, the people were being better educated than they were before. The Liberal party passed a great measure of educational reform in 1870, and be could tell them what had happened in consequence. In 1869 there were 10,327 inspected schools in this kingdom; in 1880 there were 20,670. In 1869 the scholars numbered 1,332,000, and ia 1880 3,155,000. (Cheers.) They were increasing. The Liberal party.had done a great deal to pro- .. .. . . . . . .
vide the People with political knowledge. They had seen the effects of the taxes upon knowledge, as it was called. . .
He remembered.perfeetly.well when. there was a small news-

paper printed with a Government stamp in the corner. So much duty was charged for every advertisement in it, so much was charged for the paper, and the result was that they had to pay sixpence for a very small sheet. As a matter of course, there were then few newspapers. He would
tell them what was the ease now. In 184.6 'there were 14 daily newspapers, in 1880 there were 166. In 1846 the total

number of newspapers was 531, now there were 1,886. And not only was there a greater number of newspapers, but every one of them was circulated to a much greater extent than use to be the case with those miserable papers that he remembered when a boy, and people were able to read them, and did read them, and the result was that they took a lively interest in political affairs. Of course they had . . .

meetings and attended them, and liked to hear politic-al sub- jects discussed; and he must say he thought it was a very good thing, because political agitation was a necessity for the life of the Liberal party—(applause)--far more than the . .

Tory party. The Tori• pfs 'stood, by class and privileges. They required no agitation. If they found a number of men who had a common interest, they would find that they bound themselves together and supported that interest with- out any political agitation. He observed that Lord Carnar- von a few weeks ago in the course of a speech, made this remark—" This much I will say, whatever our faults may be, the Conservative party, as a party, have no selfish ob- jects to gain." (Laughter.) He had a great respect for Lord Carharvon and thought that he was a con- scientious man who would not tell an-audience whatlibe did not believe; but he thought he was a weak man, and he (Mr. Rylands) must say his lordship must have persuaded himself by some peculiar power that 3 state of things existed which was entirely contrary to what they knew did exist; contrary to the history of politics in this kingdom. Selfish objects had been a bond of union with the Conservative party for years gone past. . .
(Hear, hear, anfi applause.) Every great struggle in favour of popular progress-bad been a struggle against selfish class . . . . . . . , . .

interests that had been maintained be! the Conservative party. Open ports, the possession of slaves, and all other abuses that existed in the State were fought for by the Con- servative party, because they were identified with class in- terests, and they—the Liberal, the Radical party—(cheers) —had fought against those class privileges and interests, and first to the extent that they had succeeded they had gained a boon, not to a class, but to the great body of,their fellow-countrymen. (Applause.) Talk of Conservatives having no selfish interests, no selfish objects to gain—why, let them look at the army, the navy, the Church, at the land, and in every one of these departments they would find there were class privileges that the Tories were maintaining and• the Liberals were challenging, and they might also rely upon it that so long as the people of this country were ignorant and apathetic the Tory party would be perfectly satisfied. (Laughter and applause.) They bad nothing to fear so long as that state of things existed, and it was only by political discussion by political movement, by political agitation, that the Liberals were able to produce an impres- sion upon that serried rank of powerful interests that was maintaining privileges which were not to the advantage of the public at large. (Hear, hear.) There was, at all events, this satisfaction in the great number of public meetings which were being held at the present time; but there was a great contrast between the lines of political information which now were prevalent and those that existed three years ago. Looking back three years, to the time when Lord Beaconsfield had the rule of this country, let them 'think what was happening at that period of political discus- sion. Let them remember that in three quarters of the globe there were lowering clouds that threatened danger and storms; that in three quarters of the globe the British power was being exerted for immoral and for dangerous objects. If they looked in Europe they saw the British power, not on the side of liberty, but supporting Turkish despotism by its diplomacy, and destroying the hopes of those rtruggling Christian nationalities that were seeking to throw off the Turkish yoke. They found our Government so anxious to promote its own selfish• interests that it was prepared to sacrifice the right of nationalities in Europe; and stimula- ting an insane dread of Russia, creating that Russophobia in order that it might make certain moves een the political chessboard of Europe which were not to the advantage of the people of Europe at large. (Applause.) He contrasted at length the foreign policy of the past with that of the present Government, showing how that the policy of the Liberal Government was one of peace, and pointed out its effects upon trade. Referring to the agricultural interests at home, he said they had to meet a foreign competition of a very severe character; and they had food, corn, and cattle intro- duced at prices which had pressed very much upon the rates which farmers in this country had been able to get for their produce; and in addition to the pressure of foreign competition, they had unfortunately had three or four bad harvests, the effect of which had been very disastrous, and in the judgment of very competent persons had entailed a loss in this country of 120 to 130 millions of money. He tobserved the other day that a very distinguished member of Parliament—Sir Thomas Acton—a leading agriculturist and a land owner, made a speech on the land question, in the course of which, alluding to the great pressure on the land, he said what he (Mr. Rylands) thought they might all be- lieve, that the present land laws had, to a greater or less extent, broken down. Further, he said, "The two main questions are these—first, are the owners of the soil of Eng.: land in the best position for doing that which their country has a reasonable right to expect of them? Secondly, are the occupying cultivators ot the eon in the position of security which they have a right, to expect, in order to con- duct their business with comfort and success to themselves?" He (Mr. Rylands) had no hesitation in answering both questions in the negative. The country had a right to expect from the owners of the soil that they would find capital for the permanent buildings and other improvements, and that they would' so use their land as to secure to the public the greatest amount of produce. This would become very shortly an important question; and it was important, in looking at the land tueetion, to bear in mind that the pro- perty in land was very different*om that in anything else. The highest authorities told them that land was held sub- ject to certain trusts, and that these trusts most be fulfilled before the land could be diverted to any mere fancy purpose , that its owner might wish to apply it to. Judge Longfield, of the Irish Encumbered Estates Court, said land was the I gift of the Creator to all men, and was held in order that it I might be cultivated to the best advantage. (Hear, bear.) The country had a right, having regard to the trust in which land was held, to inquire if the landowners fulfilled the trust. Had the seil been properly cultivated, and was it 90 held as to produce the greatest quantity of food to the community at large? The soil did not produce the quan- tity of food which it ought to produce in the interests of the community at large, and he quoted evidence on the subject. Mr. Tomkinson told, t'aern the agricultural produce of the country amounted to £300,000,000. He (Mr. Rylands) had an estimate by Mr. Cairn to the effect that the annual pro- duce of wheat, barley, oats, &c; was 87,000,000; potatoes, 161 ; butchers' meat, bacon, and ham, and other articles, 157 millions; making a total of 261 millions sterling. Let them imagine the effect if under any system of land tenure the produce of the soil could be doubled— that was, in addition to the 260,000,000 now produced, an- other 260,000,000 could be produced. Could they form any conception'of what the effect would be on the home trade of the country? It was utterly impossible to realise he effect. He believed the effect would be enormous. It would do very much to create employment, it would pro- mote the advantages of the agriculturalists, and would be of the greatest possible assistance to the people in the manufacturing districts, because the agricultural districts would form the best home market for manufactured goods t and in that respect it was clear the interests of agriculture and manufacture were one and the same. (Hear, hear.) They all had one and the same interest; that being so they should, as far as possibla, promote the opening of the home market for manufactured produce. (Cheers.) The justifi- cation of the present system of holding land was that the landowners should be in the position to make the necessary improvements and to supply capital for the development of the land in the best possible way. But it was not so. and he would tell them why. The reason was that our laws had been so framed ea eo tie up as far as possible the land in large estates, and the estates had gone on increasing, and the result was now that 10,207 persons owned two-thirds of England and Wales; 330 persons owned two-thirds of Scot- land ; and 1,942 persons owned two-thirds of Ireland. He said that they must get rid of settlements as well as the law of primogeniture, and they must insist on absolute ownership of the land; and if a man did not pay his debts let the land be sold. (Cheers.) Tben, in addition to that, be had a strong opinion that it would be very much less in the interest of this country if all estates, encumbered beyond a certain point were placed in a court to be sold—he believed they should come to that—(a voice: "Whit ought to be," and applause)—lnd he hoped, whenever they did come to that, that the tenants on the estates would have the right of pre-emption, and that the Government would be prepared to assist them, with the view of creating a yeomanry class again. (Cheers.) Let them look at the numerous accounts of the sufferings from depression and losses experienced by farmers. He thought there were signs that the farmers would not consent to be bamboozled by Tory landowners much longer. (Hear, hear, and cheers.) They had been taking quack medicines for a long time—(laughter)—but now therr condition was so serious that they would insist on an entire change of treatment, aud would demand a great reform of the land laws, seas to give security for their capital invested in the land. (Hear, hear, and loud, cheers.)A vote of thanks to and confidence in Mr. James romMn- sun was proposed by Mr. THOMAS A RROWSSII:rIf, and seconded by Mr. Jome CHALLONER, and carried with acclamation. A vote of thanks to Mr. Rylands was pro- posed by Mr. F. Finny, and seconded by Mr. JOHN SIMP- SON ; and three cheers for the Chairman brought the proceedings to a close. enthead At Llangollen on Wednesday the tworphaetrresbd t. o e o h housemaid and valet—charged with being concerned in the theft of jewels valued at between £40,000 and X 50,000 from the mansion ofTlehoerpdrTosreeevuotriownewreasagstaillnl unprepared with the case, and the Bench granted a further remand with reluctance,

THE DEBATING SOCIETY DISSOLVED. The last meeting of the Warrington Parliamentary Debat- ing Society was held in the Co-operative Hall, on Monday evening, tinder the presidency of Dr. Huson-More. There was a scanty attendance. The Assistant Clerk (Mr. Fair- dough) read the financial statement which showed a balance in favour of the society of £3 is. 60.—The Premier (the Rev. R. Pitcher) said he had carefully reviewed the whole circumstances, and he must say advisedly, for his own part, he had nothing to retract and nothing to regret beyond the fate of the society. (Hear, hear.) He could not help feeling that the offence came not from their side, but sprang from misrepresentation in the first place, and that they could not with regard for their own right, free thought, -and free speech, admit for one moment the pretensions Made , en the other side. (Hear, hear.) It had been thrown at time that he was not, in favour of healing the breach. He did nothing to give that impression, though he frankly admitted he was not in favour of it. He felt that if these gentlemen were to come back it would, only be at the cost of free thought and free speech, without which, Liberalism at least, could not exist. (Applause.) He might say in Self defence, he had made up his mind—though this was the first time that he had ever said it—quietly to withdraw if those gentle- men returned, for never could he consent to face foes So utterly unworthy of his steel. (Hear, hear.) In order to test the feeling of the House he proposed the society be dis- solved, that of the balance in hand, the sum of Ll, be handed to the Sergeant at Arms in recognition of his services— (hear, hear)—and that the secretary be instructed to pay the residue cf the balance to the Warrington Infirmary. (Applause.) His reasons for doing this was that it was quite possible there might be souse portion of the Tory property in the balance they had left, and although he main- tained that the society still existed and had full power over all monies belonging to it, it would save any possible mis- representation if they selected the Infirmary, in which both they and their friends, the enemy, took an interest. Having finished his last official act in retiring from the premiership of the society, and from the leadership of the Liberal party, he begged very heartily to thank them for the confidence which they had placed in him. He was fully conscious he had tried to do his best, and he trusted their parting would be as cordial on their side as he was sure it was on his. {Applause.) The Conservative member for Wenlock (Mr. Machen) seconded the proposition. He agreed with what had been suggested as to the disposal of the funds, and hoped a cordial spirit towards one another would always prevail. The two or three Conservatives who had remained thought the Liberals had not treated them so discourteously as their leader wauld have them believe. (Applause.)—The Home Secretary (Mr. H. Roberts), who had attempted to heal the breach, said hedid not think he was betraying any secret when he said he found at the meeting of the Council, which was held immediately after the rupture, such a spirit of de- termined opposition and repudiation of their proposals to- wards conciliation on the part of the Leader of the Op- position, that ha was convinced it was perfectly hopeless to allow matters to proceed further in the way of obtaining a settlerhent. He found also that the Liberal party could not with a,true recognition of its own dignity go further in that direction, and he felt he must withdraw from any further at- tempt to patch up matters. He said nothing whatever which needed to have alarmed them, or made them frightened of tbe position they occupied that evening. The action of the Conservative party was unbecoming and childish in the ex- treale, and he was afraid if he could only come at the facts the Conservative party wanted a reason for leaving the society. (Applause.) He believed they felt themselves thoroughly overmastered, not only in numbers, but intellect and argument, and they were afraid of conversions taking place. It behoved them to provide some other means for spreading information amongst themselves. It was some satisfaction to him to know the leaders of the Conservative party were not worthy of the name. In conclusion, he referred to the statement made by the Opposition respecting the action of the Speaker, which action he maintained was beyond question. The member for South East Lancashire (Mr. T. Birchall) supported the proposition, and cordially endorsed the statements of the last speaker.—The members , for Norwich, Boston, Newcastle-on-Tyne, Merthyr Tydvil, Dudley, dr.c., expressed their regret at the dissolution of the society, and the proposition was carried unanimously.— Votes of thanks were tendered to the Deputy Clerk of the House, and the Speaker, and the society, which started , under the most favourable auspices, was dissolved.

div.p: WARRINGTON INFIRMARY CONCERT.

On Saturday evening, a concert was given in the Public Hall, at the instance of the Workingmen's Committee of the Warrington Infirmary, with the object of raising a sum of money to- be given to the institution as the workingmen's subscription. His worship the Mayor, J. R. Pickmere, Esq , presided over the evening's proceedings, and, after apolo- gising for the absence of several gentlemen who had expected to be present, proceeded to give a short sketch of the history of the Infirmary, and pointed out the laudable purpose for which the concert was being given: He said he accepted the invitation to preside with much pleasure. He was present with Mr. Armitage at the first meeting of working- men, which was largely attended, in the Mayor's parlour lost year. It was then arranged that a committee should be formed, of which 'Mr. John Roberts was elected chairman, for the purpose of soliciting subscriptions from those parties who had not hitherto subscribed. The result was that nearly £2OO had been obtained for the funds of the institute. (Applause.) The concert that night was to assist this fund, and he was delighted to see so large an audience present in spite of the inclemency of the weather. He hoped every indulgence would be granted to the ladies and gentlemen who had kindly given their services, as all knew that a dense fog was not favourable to vocal powers. He hoped the zeal of the Workingmen's Committee would not flag, but that the working classes would contribute their mites and he begged to thank them for what they had so well done, and to wish them every success in the future. (Applause.) The artistes consisted chiefly of local amateurs. Mr. R. H. Pearson who engaged as violinist and Mr. Geo. Riley under- took the duties of conductor and accompanist. There was a large audience, and a pleasing programme was performed. Miss Hind sang with excellent taste " Truant love " (Cowan), and gained an_encore, and subsequently in "The lady of the Lea," though not equally successful in pleasing the audience, she did full justice to a song the coaintness of which is not often fully disclosed in amateur renderings. Some allowance for a badly chosen song must be made in the case of Miss Burrows' first' effort. " Bid me discourse" presents difficulties in the way of florid phrases with which manifestly she lacked confidence to overcome altogether successfully. Nevertheless h r singing evinced much pains- taking earnestness and fair vocal ability. "A bird in hand" was tastefully rendered by Mrs. Pearson and gained an encore. Another of this series of proverb songs was also given by Mrs. Pearson in the second part of the programme, and its performance was greeted with loud applause. Mr. Eccles sang "The old sexton" with appropriate expression, but the song proved a little tedious in point of length. "The diver' ( oder,) is pecu- liarly adapted for displaying the depth and sonorousness of Mr. Eccles' voice, and his interpretation of this song left little room for improvement. The duet by Miss Hind and Mr. Eccles was excellently rendered and received well merited applause. Mr. Dell's singing is not altogether pleasing by reason of the inherent defects of his voice. But making due allowance for natural disadvantages Mr. Dell is fairly successful before an audience, his songs always shew- ing an honest endeavour to convey the sentiment. "I seek for thee in every flower," is a favourite song of Mr. Dell's, in which he always succeeds in securing warm applause. In response to en encore he substituted "My pretty Jane." Mr. Geo. Wright gave some nautical songs in a vigorous style and in robust baritone voice. Under these conditions songs of this character never fail to find favour with a popular as- sembly. The present instance formed no exception to this broad rule, considerable enthusiasm being shewn in regard to Mr. Wright's songs. The violin solos served to diver- sify an otherwise monotonous array" of songs in the pro- gramme. Mr. Pearson played with his wonted skill and taste. In the lighter passages requiring dexterity and neat execution especially, Mr. Pearson is quite at home. The fantasia and airs with variations set down to his name in the programme were therefore suited to his forte and the re- sult was highly gratifying to the audience. Mr. Williams and Mr. Mercer contributed some comic items with marked I iccess. The result of the concert is a sum of some £3O to be handed to the Infirmary arid we are sure that the working- men's committee are grateful to the various artistes through whose gratuitious services the concert has been lrought to so successful an issue. id I sew

Mr. Walter Powell, M.P. for Malmesbury, and two friends attempted to make an ascent in a balloon, at Bridport, on Saturday night, when the car dragged along the ground, throwing Mr. Powell's companions out, one being seriously injured. The balloon then rose again, went across the channel, and when last seep was descending to the water. Darkness then bid it from view, and nothing has since been heard of the intrepid aernant, though every effort has been' put forth to compass his safety. Nothing has been heard of the Saladin or Mr. Wm. Powell, M.P., and Captain Templer has now arrived at the conclusion that the balloon did descend into the sea, and not, as he first thought, ascend and cross the Channel. There is no additional information respecting the balloon which it was reported was sees cross- ing from the sea over Hartlepool on Tuesday. A telegram from Guernsey states that some French fishermen have re- ported seeing a balloon drifting towards the south-west near Roches Douvres, and search vessels started on Wednesday fl the direction indicated.

BRUNSWICK MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT CUSS. MR. SHORE ON THE ORIGIN OF SURNAMES. On Wednesday eyening there was a very good attendance at the above claw, when Mr. W. J. Shore read a very in- teresting paper, en' itled, "The origin of surnames." Mr. dimister presided.—Mr. SHORE said that to review the nomenclature of a nation was to review the history of that nation, and to deal with the surnames of 23,000,000 of people wassail onerous task; but it was not to be supposed that he was about to explain the origin of all names. He only hoped to show them the skeletons upon which sur- names were adjusted, and having done that, leave the ad- justment of similar s.:rnamea to the audience. In the early stages of the world, it was found that one name was suffi- cient, as Adam, Jacob, Jeremiah, &c., which names were derived from some circumstances closely connected with the individual. But a little study would prove that even then it was found desirable, and indeed needful, that they ohould.4 have some method by which they could distinguish one Joseph from another, so as to give them greater indi- viduality. To remedy this, such expressions as " Joshua, the son of Nun," "Joseph, of Arimatlicea," " sir"°n, the tanner," "Simon Zelotes," &a., were used. The want of surnames in the Jewish nation was obviated, as it was suffi- cient to name the tribe to which a man belonged to indicate .as hn the case of which Joseph or Peter was referred to, "Simon, of_Cyrene." It was not until thetunwaesofttohebeßfoomuannls that a perfect system of nornenclature .d Qeming to the early histbry of Britain, he said the Saxons were known only by names which changed from father to SOD, as was te be found in one of. the earliest records, which referred to the marrriage 0f Tom Johnson, the son of Richard Thomson." About the time of the conquest, through the increase of commerce and the need of written documents, surnames began to be used by universal consent. These they derived from different sources, which might be divided Into five clever: Baptismal, local, official, occu- pative, and soubriquet, or nicknames. It was necessary to carefully examine , the Christian names then •in use, as it was from these that the largest proportion of surnames originated. They might take for instance the Dame' William. It was a custom at the present day to shorten the word into Willie, but such was not the hahit at the period he had been alluding to. Then they affixed such words as "kin, cock, ot, et, on, and en." By looking at this system for a while it was easily under- stood how Simon became Simkin, or Simcock. Thonans might, by the same method, become Thompkins or Thomp- kinson, the son of Thompkins. William might also become Wilcock, Wilcox, Williamson, Wilkins, &c., and from John proceeded the names Jones, Johnson, Jenks, Jenkins, Ivan, Evans, or Bevan, Welsh for John, Hanson, Hancock, Ilan- kinson, from the Flemish, Micklejohn, or little John, Robert became Robin hence Robinson, &c. Howardcarne fromthe name Herewak a name used before the Conquest. The name of the deity Thor, was seen in Thorley, Thurlow, Thorold, &c. From the names Geoffrey, Fulke, and Henry, which were much in use at the time of Henry IL, came the following names :—From Geoffrey: Jeffs, Jeffries, Jeffer- son, Jepson, Jrc. From Fulke : Foulkes, Fawkes, and Follies. It was but natural that the locality where a person was born or lived should offer a satisfactory means of creating an individuality for him. For instance, the new, John Wood carried its own significance. And hirst, which bad formerly meant a coppice, was now used as a surname. From that they derived the names, Hazlehurst, Ashnrst, Lyndhurst, ilawkhurst, and Deuhurst, den meaning a small vale. Such names as Clough, Cliff, Combs, Acre, Mountain, Hill, and Field needed no explanation. Parnell came from Fetronella, Glatistone from Glede-stone, Welsh, Inglis, Morris, Norman, Brittin, Gaskin, Burgon, and Lyons all came with foreigners from the cities w,hoie names they resembled. The official names were as follows :—King, Justice, Demer, or Rempster, Serjeant, Beadell, Catchpole, Crier, Priestman, and Deakin, A considerable number of the ancient feudal offices were also fossilled in the names of , the country. A few examples would suffice. Porter, Chamberlain, Barber, Simister frorPi Summaster, who held the office of paymaster; Spearman, Bowman, Archer, Jrc. Forrester, Warrtier, Thackeg or Thatcher, Tyler, Coward, from Cow-herd, Calf-herd, Oxen-herd, Day- man or Dairyman Milne, Arkwright, Smith, because he smites the anvil, pedler, Packer, &c., all come from the various occupations then carried on by the individuals who bore them. The last eass of names was the sobriquet or nickname. From such sources many names were obtained.' A person's peculiarities were thus immortalised in his name, as in the following instances :—Crowfoot, Goosebeak, Bull- head, Scuttlernouth, Swetinbed, Drinkdregges, Drybred Doo- little, Scatteriood, &c. Jrc. The word "leg," as applied to the natural propeller Of the body, was not in vogue in Britain before the Norwegians introduced it, so that the word shanks was used, and it was responsible for some of the peculiar sur- names at present afloat, such as Cruikshank, Lougshanks, and Sheepshanks. Mr. Shore here introduced an aniusing anecdote. A Mr. Sheepshanks, of Jesus College, pronounced the word satire satyr, and a wag wrote the following poetry, to the great chagrin of the victim : The satyrs of old were satyrs of note, With the head of a man they'd the shanks of a goat; But the satyr of Jesus all satyrs surpasses, Whilst his shanks are a sheep's, his head is an ass's. Another list of names came from the word head. From this source emanated Downyhead, Ruffhead, Hardhead, White- &c. Mr. Shore thought Lb& owners of high-sounding names didn't need to feel proud of them, for there were many cases on record of persons who bore good and noble names diegraeinh them ; and it was also a fact that the greatest and noblest among the benefactors of the country were men who bore some of the more ignoble names.— A Tote of thanks was accorded to Mr. Shore for his services.

RUNCORN. The Runcorn volunteers, F and G companies, attended Diviae service at the Parish Church, on Sunday morning, under the command of Captain Hazlehurst. There were also present—Colonel J. Ashton and Captains Kerr and R. Ashton. The total strength was 82, including the band, and the men presented their customary smart appearance. The Rev. Canon Barclay, hon. chaplain, who preached for the rst time for several months, and whose restored health will give rise to much pleasure, took for his text," So Jonathan became mighty, because he prepared his ways before the Lord his God." He spoke of that December day when the earliest members of the corps assembled at the Town Hall to take the oath of allegiance to the Queen, and although there were now very few still in the ranks, yet they had been reinforced from time by fresh recruits, and they con- tinued to be a settled institution of the town, and in time of iloger they might calculate upon the pluck and patrietism of their gallant volunteers. Although the danger of the foreign invasion which first drew the force into existence was now over, who knew but how soon it might again return. England was hardly any longer an island, and the " silver streak," which in times past was considered to be their defence, was no longer a certain defence against an invading foe. Powerless though they might be to interfere in the cause of European right, let them ever remember that she must not be powerless for the mightiest self-defence. If Sparta of old considered that the best bulwark lay in the breasts cf her citizens, let them also be determined that their bulwark should be the same living bastion of impregnable defence. If their navy could no longer sweep the seas with irresistible might, if the days of the Nile and Trafalgar were I but memories of past pre-eminence, let them at any rate determine that the days of the Armada should be theirs as 'Fon°. as the seas beat upon the English cliffs. England her- self any rate must be as the "strong man armed whose goods are in peace." Otherwise she was not safe. Let her once become as weak as she was wealthy,let her become not envied but hated, let her become not only disregarded but despised, and be would be a simpleton who would think that she would not become a prey to the machinations of her -enemies; so that volunteers were not only of service to their country, they were necessary. In the day of peril they would be the country's main defence, because they would add discipline to courage and skill to strength. If the coun- try were invaded, which God forbid, rio doubt her arms; ' would fight until in the last forlorn hope the last man fell. Their very peasautry would arm themselves in defence of their hearths and homes. He would, however, remind them that the spirit that should al ways animate them should be the spirit ef dependence upon a higher Arm than an arm of flesh, and that they should not forget that there was a higher power than that of the rifle and bayonet. Their presence in the house of God that day showed that they were animated with the spirit of pace. It augured well for the cause they had in hand that they would unite piety to prowess and Christianity to courage. The strength ef an empire was in God, yet how slow were monarchs and ministers to recognise this. It had often been their custom almost gaily and cheerily tO submit their quar- rels to the derision of the sword, but all the time He who sat upon the circle nf the world was not an unconcerned spectator of the world's doings. Volumes had been written to account for a nation's rise or fall, but if they looked at the history of nations in the light of God's Word they would find an exemplification of the truth of the text, that that nation only became mighty, when it prepared its ways before tbe Lord its God. Ancient Tyre was now a place of desola- tion and solitude. Spain was so degraded that even the petty princes of Europe had despised her proffered crown. Thiswas true in the case of individuals as well as of nations; and bethought that that soldier who was the most earnest servant of his God would prove the most worthy in his country's defence. He advised them to strive against un. godliness. drunkenness, and wickedness of all kinds, so that when the last word of command was given theifs might be tplee,experienee of that soldier who in his dying moments in his bed with almost supernatural strength, rose up on back., c 511)znal :tilt criedy wilaleartsaakhreec.drieih.'.' div.p: WIDNES POLICE COURT, , MownAv.—Before Mr. Holbrook Gaskell, jun. A Poon FELLOW WITH" A BEN IN 1119 Bowtner.7--Frank Williams was charged with being an insane person at large, at Widnes, on the previous Saturday.—lt appeared that on the day in question P.C. McDonald saw the prisoner stand- ing about in Mersey-road. He thought that his manner seemed very strange. He stood for an hour together in the street perfectly motionless, though the night was a very cold one. When questioned as to who he was and what he was doing there, hc was unable to give any clear and satis- factory answer, and seemed half-witted. It appears that subsequently, when he had been locked up by P.C. Mc- Donald, he told Inspector Barnett that his father was a manager in the Potteries, where his home was. He seemed to perfectly realise the fact that he was of weak intellect, they oyyhf a had haudanc tot telegraphed lfmes goua rmnraci epchohai ntteeeedcd arrived t :taw ceikt. and attributed the cause to his having spent too much time sandp friendse e ttoor labourhave va trehinnhee tispn itt rusi tdstaoai tenkeseed, rn,e tsahpncaeadter ietialhel - -h theia toask- ing L fetch I:dim—The prisoner was therefore handed over to his

- friends. WEDNESDAY.—Before Messrs. W. L. Evans (chairman), John Brock, and Holbrook Gaskell, jun. SERIOUS OFFENCE UNDER THE PAWNBROKERS' ACT.— Miss Annie Jamieson was summoned under the Pawnbrokers' Act, for having receiyed a pledge from a child six years of age.—An officer was called who stated that about a quarter to two, on the afternoon of the 6th inst., he s'aw the girl coming out of defendant's shop, and on going inside Miss Jamieson admitted having received a pledge from her.—Mr. W. T. Husband defended, and said Mrs. Jamieson, mother of defendant, was well known in Widnes to be a very respectable lady. Ile believed the police were quite willing to admit that she had for six or seven years carried on her business in a most careful manner. The pledge eves received from a woman named Conner, who was often so ill as to be unable to leave her bed: Nothing of the kind would be allowed again.—Mr. Lewin (magistrates' clerk) said the defendant was liable to a fine of £lo.—The Chairman said the offence was a most serious one, but as thin Wits defendant's first summons she would only be fihed 205., and 19s. COMB. AFFILIATION ARREARS—AIfred Pownall was sent to gaol two mouths for neglecting to pay upwards of £4 affiliation arrears. ALLEGED WOUNDING 'WITH A KNlFE.—David 'Hatton, dressed as a sailor, was charged with unlawfully wounding a man named William Macnamara.—Sergeant Robinson gave evidence as to apprehending the prisoner; and Dr. Cooper saidthe complainant's wounds were so serious that he was not able to appear.—Prisoner was remaaded until Tuesday. A POLICEMAN "WITH HIS EYES ABOUT HlM."—William Dwyer, a dirty looking fellow, was charged with assaulting P.C. Charles Anderson.—The officer stated that about a quarter to seven on the previous night he sew the prioner coming out of Messrs. Mnspratt's yard carrying a bundle of wood, which, on seeing that he was watched, he dropped and ran off. He followed him, and succeeded in capturing him, on which Dwyer seized him by the legs, threw him down, and kicked him. The prisoner was only secured with the assistance of P.C.'s McGee and Ormrod.—Sent to gaol one mouth with hard labour. THE SUPERINTENDENT'S RAID ON THE SPIRIT SELLERS. —Samuel Dagnall, keeper of the Northirich Vaults, was summoned for selling to Superintendent Barker three half pints of Irish whiskey and three half pints of rum, which were not of the nature, substance, and quality of the articles demanded.—Mr. Barker said he visited defendant's on the 10th, and purchased the whiskey for Sc. He then explained that he had bought it for the purpose of sending it to the County Analyst, and offered to divide it into three parts, leaving Dagnel one. He also bought the rum, and made defendant a similar offer. He forwarded the spirit to the Public Analyst.—Sergeant Ball gave corroborative evid- ence in this and the following cases.—Mr. Lewin (magistrates' clerk) read the analyst's certificate, which stated that the rum was 381 per cent. under proof, or 131 per cent, beyond the utmost limit allowed by , the Amendment Act. The whiskey was 28 per cent. under proof.—Mr. Bartlett, of Liverpool, defended in this and the other canes, and contended that it was highly probable the extreme lowness of the spirits under proof was owing to the peculiar circumstances under which they were analysed. In the one case defendant was fined £5 and costs (135.), and in the other 20e. and costs.--John Anderson, of the Com- mercial Inn, was charged with selling the Superiptendent three half-pints of ram, under similar circumstances, on the 10th ult.—Mr. Barker proved the purchase of the spirit for 2s. 6d., which Mrs. Anderson said would have been Sc. if he had wanted it bottling.—Mr. Lewin read the certificate of Mr. Campbell Brown, which showed that the spirit was 361 per cent, under proof, and 14 per cent, below the limit of strength permitted by the Act.—Mr. Bartlett observed that it was no use for him to reiterate his arguments. He might, however, say that the offence was not a venal one, for from a teetotal point of view, the defendant was really doing the man to whom he sold the spirit good, by weakening it ! Defendant was fined £4 and 13s. costs.—John Smith, of the Railway Hotel, was also summoned on a like charge.— The Superintendent said he visited defendant's, on the 10th ult., and purchased from his wife a quantity of Irish whiskey, which was forwarded to be analysed.—Mr. Lewin said the certificate of Dr. Brown showed the whiskey to be 33.8 per cent. under proof, or upwards of 81 per cent. below the strength permitted by the Amendment Act. Mrs. Smith was called to prove there was a printed notice in the place where the spirit was purchased which read "All spirits sold here are diluted with water."—Mr. Bartlett said that 25 degrees =de; proof was right for rum or whiskey, as that I was considered not to be to the prejudice of the purchaser, according to the Amendment Act. He maintained that the notice cleared the defendant from liability.—After consider- able consultation, the Bench said that, looking at the case alt round, they felt bound to convict, as even the exhibition, of a printed notice could not justify a publican in selling spirits so much under proof. Defendant would be fined 20a. and costs; and if Mr. Bartlett asked for a case, in order to I appeal to a superior court, they would grant him one. A GIRL CHARGED WITH BREAKING INTO A HOIISE.—' Sarah Kerley, a respectably-dressed girl, aged 15, was charged with having, on the 6th June, during the day time, broken into the dwelling-house of John Ward, and stolen a lady's gold dress ring, and two pieces of Maltese lace, value £2 14s.—Mr. Moore, Warrington defended.—The prosecu- tor is a pawnbroker, living at 31, Victoria-street, and the stolen articles are the property of his grand-daughter, Miss Mary Ann Hampson. The father of the prisoner is at pre- sent in gaol, and she is one of a family of ten children, and was formerly a member of the choir at St. Mary's Catholic Chapel. The evidence showed that on the div of the rob- bery, Miss Ilampson went out about nine in the morning, and did not return until ten in the evening. As soon as she had done so, the prisoner, who lives next door, spoke to her over the yard wall, asking if she had been home during the afternoon to play the piano, as she had heard some one in the house. On going upstairs Miss Hampsen found her I work box had been broken open, and the things mentioned in the charge stolen. A Mrs. Brocklebank, of Cholmondley- street, saw the prisoner with the ring in a house in the same street, on the day of the robbery. She professed to have bought it for a shilling. On P.C. Clarkson examiring the prosecutor's house, shortly after the robbery, he fonnclinarks on the sash of it having been tampered with.—Mr. Moore ridiculed the idea of a girl of such tender wee having broken into the house.—The magistrates committed her for trial at the Liverpool Quarter Sessions.

• RUNCORN PAULI A MENTARY - DEBATING SOCIETY. An unusual number of Conservative members turned up on Tuesday evening, at the meeting of this society, in an- anticipation of hearing the final debate on the Parliamentary Disabilities Bill, but the Liberals were not quite so strong numerically as they are sometimes.—After the questions had been disposed of, the leader of the opposition, in a somewha eloquent and exhaustive speech, commenced the adjourned debate on the bill for the removal of Parliamentary disab- ilities, which be strongly opposed, and was supported by the member for Nottingham.—The Premier said he sympathized very considerably with;the leader of Her Majesty's opposition in the hesitating manner ;n which he had given his views. As far as he could see the principles and the details of the bill were left intact. They bad been twitted on that side of the House by the right hon. gentleman with having failed to bring in the measures promised in the Queen's speech, namely :—furthering the extension of a national system of education, the conditions under which land is at present held and cultivated; the representation of the people by a re-distribution of seats, the incidence of local taxation, and the establishment of representative County Boards. He thought if the right hon. gentlemen would brush up his recollection, he would remember it was the result of a certain conversation between themselves, and if there was any res- ponsibility to be shred, he thought it ought to be shared by the leader of the opposition as well us himself. The right hon. gentleman was here interrupted by the leader of the opposition who rose to make an explanation. He stated the conversation which had been spoken of was by no means in an official or political capacity. The Premier accepted the explanation and said be would say nothing further about it. Referring to the bill then before Parliament he said every man of a full age and sound mind when duly elected by a constituency ought to be free and was free legally to take his seat in the House of Commons. The member for Win- chester a few sittings ago told them the question had resolved itself into a matter of altering the constitution; he (the Premier) thought the constitution required raking up so that it might yield more abundantly for future generations.—The member for Oxford said be had great pleasure in moving the adjournment of the debate amidst cries of "Divide, divide" from the opposition benches. This had the effect of causing the utmost consternation among the members on the Gov- side of the House, and especially when the speaker an- nounced that he had no alternative but to call upon the I Home Secretary to reply if the Conservatives insisted upon it. Liberals might be walking to and fro in a very excited state of mind whilst others were apparently agitated and crest-fallen. The conservatives were rubbing their hands in high glee with faces beaming with radiance, thinking the long looked for defeat was at hand. This however was not to be, for when the inevitable division was taken there were 11 votes for the adjournment against P. When this dis- closure was announced the Conservatives felt themselves thoroughly overwhelmed and retired in bitter disappointment. The Pelle was turned in consequence of the clerk of the House inadvertently giving his card to the wrong teller which apparently pleased the liberals, as it placed them in a majority, and prevented the tediousness of a long, if not an all night sitting.
A WIDNES LABOURER DROWNED.
CENSURE ON THE CANAL COMPANY. mond& afternoon an inquest was held at the Main

Top Inn, Mersey-road, Widnes, by Mr. Barker, deputy coroner, on the body of John McGregor, aged 17, a labourer, of N 0,15, Davies-street. Mr. Barker said deceased was last seen alive at about six o'clock on Saturday morning, when he was on the way to his work, and crossing the bridge leading over the canal;to Messrs. Gossages' soap works, when he was drowned. It appeared that the morning was foggy, and a search was made for deceased, but he could not be found. Snspicion was then aroused that he had got into the canal, and an enquiry was instituted, which resulted in his body being found in the water at about noon of the same day. Evidence would be brought forward to show that the man carried a lamp attached to his waist, and they would probably arrive at the conclusion that he fell into the canal during the fog. They would, therefore, probably conclude to return a verdict of "Found drowned." Ho was glad to say that no marks of violence were found on the person of the deceased, and there was no suspicion of foul play, so that the enquiry would, in all probability, not prove a lengthy one. Thomas Tomlinson, a flatman, of Sankey Bridges, de- posed that on Saturday morning, about a quarter to twelve o'clock, he was on the west side of Widnes locks, on the St. Helens and Widnes canal, searching for a boat, when a lad told him he was grappling for deceased When -he got to the spot where the work was going on, he told the people that they wolld .find the body much sooner if they would use a boat book. It was agreed that be should try and get olickand he went to a flat called the Maria Louisa for that pritpose. He succeeded in finding the boat hook, and after feeling at the bottom of the canal for a little while, he said, "It's no use feeling any further, because he is here," and he pulled the poor fellow's' body out by the wasteband of his trousers. Deceased was found_ about ten or fifteen yards

from the lock. John Oakes, 48, Bridge-street, deposed that he was a labourer at Messrs. Gossages', and at about six o'clock on I Saturday morning he saw deceased going to his work along the canal bank, with a lamp fastened round his waist. He left him near the foot bridge which crossed the canal, and over which he would bare to pass as he was going to his • work, and he did not see him again until he was taken out of the water. Margaret Ann McGregor said deceased formerly lived with her at No. 15, Davies-street, and was a single man. She last saw him alive on Saturday morning, at about a quarter to six, when he was in the kitchen of liar house. He was quite sober when he left home to go to his work in the crystal house. at Messrs. Gessages' ; in fact, he was always very temperate. A juryman said there was no protection at the place where deceased fell into the water, and this made it very dangerous. Another Juryman: I was on an inquest in a similar case when Mr. Driffield was coroner, and it was suggested that some railings ought to be placed there. The Coroner: Would not that interfere with the towing path? Is there any. representative of the 1.. and N. W. Hy, Co. here? Mr. Bilsborough, goods and canal agent to the company at Widnes, said he was present to watch the Koceedings on - behalf of the company. The Coroner: What do you say about th't suggestion? Mr. Bilsborough : I cannot exactly say,`ras it is more a matter for the consideration of the engineer than for myself. It certainly is awkward. The Coroner: Have the public a right of footpath there? Yes; they have a perfect right of way there. Any one , can go that way.—Then of course the public should be pro- . . .

tected. A Juryman : I consider that the company are very cul- pable in not having put a protection there. James McGregor, father of deceased, gave evidence to the effect that on the morning of his death he (deceased) was in. his usual health and spirits. He had never manifested any suicidal tendency of mind. Witness then went on to say: , That canal bank is not safe for any man in winter time. On such a Moruleeg as deceased lost his life, how is a man to know at what part of the bank he is *ate and Where he is not 15°? The Coroner: How long had he Wed the canal path as i'l , road to his work? Oh, a long time. , 1 The Coroner: Then he knew tbecanal, and wasacquainted 1 with the danger of the road during such weather 2—lie had , regularly used it as a road to his work; in fact, it was the Only road. On Saturday morning, whilst I was going that way myself, when half way up the canal bank I did not know where I Was, and in order to prevent falling inter the water I had to creep upon my knees. The Coroner: I dare say it is confusing. - The witness: It is very awkward that the place should be left in the way it is. The Coroner tben summed up as follows :—Gentlemen of the jury, that is the evidence, and upon that your verdict must be one of "Found drowned." There is no evidence how deceased got into the water. It is, however, almost a moral certainty that the unfortunate man whilst in this difficult part of the catial bank must have etembled, and so fallen in. If you think that this part of the bank is in a 1 dangerous condition, it is quite within your province to make a recommendation to that effect to the Canal Company. If the road had been a private one, that course would not have been open to you; but the representative of the company who is present say:, it is an open road, and it therefore ought to be protected. At the same time, you must remember that a person who knows a road well, and takes upon himself to go that way, does so at his own risk, in some measure ; but the deceased no doubt became confused with the fog, as many people do. Of course, it was his duty to exercise care; and if he thought the way was a dangerous one, he ought to have gone by a more circuitous path. At the same time if you are of opinion that it is a dangerous place, something ought to be done. I itm very sorry to find that this is the second fatal accident which has occurred there, and that though a recommendation was made, it was not attended to. Of course, there is no doubt that juries some- times make recommendations which are not practicable or feasible; and it occurred to me during the hearing of the evidence that if something were put up at the place in the way of a protection, it would probably interfere with carry- ing on the business of the canal. If, however, a protection could be provided which would not interfere with the work-I lug of the canal, something ought certainly to be at once done, in order to make the place safe. I should be very glad to add any presentment which you may wish to make to your verdict, which, as far as this enquiry is concerned, must be an open one. Mr. Bilsborough : The spot is only about 15 yards from the lock gates, and I think that, owing to the amount of work which has to be done there, it would be a difficult thing to put up any protection. Tim BRIBERY SEISTEXCES.—Our readers will see from an' advertisement in to-day's issue that a movement has been set on foot to memorialise the Home Secretary to remit the bribery sentences. The memorialists condemn the offence Of which the prisoners are guilty, and do not impugn the sentences of the judges, but plead for the clemency of the Crown on the following grounds. let: That punishment being for two purposes, both corrective and deterrent, the terms undergone by the p isoners fulfil both purposes. 2nd That the prisoners have endured great torture and suspense by the delay of the prodeedings, the offences having been committed eighteen months ago. 3rd: That the offence was committed, not for the personal aggrandisement of the psi- soners, but at a time of great excitement and temptation. The memorials have already been signed by several Members of Parliament of all shades of opinion, including Mr. Eugene Collins, Mr. W. 11. James, Mr. Alderman McArthur, Lord Claud Hamilton, the Hon. Edward Stanhope, cbc., ttc. Copies of the memz,rials may be had on application to the Secretary, at the Committee Room, Westminster Palace Hotel, London, and it is requested they may ha returned there 1.. y the 20th inst., as it is purposed to present the t petition on the 22nd, so that the prisoners may return to families and tome bv Christmas Day,:

DZICE-STREET A-ND FRIARS' GREEN BIND OP HOPE. —The fifth of the winter -series of entertainments, in connec- tion with this society, was held in Brick-street school-room oo Tuesday, under the presidency of Mr. William Croskill. The chairman warmly advocated the Band of Hope move- ment. He hoped the children would keep their pledges, and urged those present, who had not yet signed the pledge, to do so, and they would not regret it. The programme was then , proceeded with, consisting of songs, recitations, and dialogues, the whole being brought to a close by 's humorous dialogue entitled" Mrs. Maggs is caught," which S.:lolt'S the subterfuges of a drunken wife to obtain drink unknown to her husband, and how she was unexpectedly caught. The characters were ably sustained, as seas evidenced by the wrapt attention that was given to the piece and the hearty applause accorded to the performers. He received the following reply r—" Local Govern- ment Board, Whitehall, Dec. 7, 1881.—Sir,—Mr. Dodson desires me to acknowledge the receipt of your letter of yes- terday's date respecting the proposal of the Widnee Local Board to pay a commission on obtaining a loan for the con- solidation bf existing delt. Mr. Dodson understands that the Local Board before taking any steps in the matters are desirous of obtaining from the Local Government Board an opinion as to the legality of this proposal, and so protecting themselves against a possible adverse decision of the auditor. It is, however, the invariable rule of the Local Government Board not to express any opinion beforehand in matters of this character, where the question involved is one which might be brought before them on am appeal from the auditor's decision. Were they not to adhere to this rule, when an appeal came before them, new considerations might be brought to their notice, and they might find themselves obliged to reverse the de- cision they-had formerlyearrived at. Under these circum- stances, Mr. Dodson could not add- scything to what has already been stated to the Local Board in the official cor- respondence on this subject, and he will not, therefore, incon- venience you by asking you to call upon him with regard to the case.—l, am, sir, your obedient servant, Hugh F. Seymour.—The speaker went on to observe that he was puzzled to know why the Local Government Board could not give a straightforward answer to a. straightforward question. —Mr. Getearomo : The letter means this—that they will sur- charge, but they wont advise. (Laughter.)—The CHAIRMAN : I think you would hardly have believed that any Govern- ment Board would have saddled the township with an expense of £2soa year, as they have really done in the case of Widnes, simply because they vagl not divert from a red tape custom! I hive nothing more to say about it. (Laughter.)—The 'CHAIRMAN : I think that in connection with this matter you will see how important it is. that there should be a strong body, such as an associa- tion of boards to take up such a question as this. Therefore, I think there are very few of you who will ' not agree with me that it is worth while for us to pay the sum of three guineas to become members of the Association of 'Local Boards and other Sanitary Authorities.--It was unanimously resolved that the Clerk be instructed to forward the three guineas subscription to the society; and o a the motion of Mr. Gasket!, it was agreed that the -Chairman of the Board and the Chairman of the Finance Committee be appointed a deputatime to attend the annual meeting. The following letter was read :—" Widnes, 10th December, 1881..—Sir,-1 beg to draw your attention to the present anomalous and unsatisfactory position medical men hold, to- ward one another and-their patients in the carrying on of the work of the Widnes Accident Hospital. Havfng applied td the Hospital Committee, sosue time ago, about some matter of importance, I was politely refereed to the prinbed rules, and as it is not at all improbable teehe again refeared to the same !melee, I prefer, for this and several other reasons, to address you—becanse, judging from w.z.lillat:ra/teTaorin,t,t:rtohuorrysh the medium of Ow press, of your public life, you alwa7 s give a fair, goe,eteele, Ond courteous con e

matters immediately connected'vvith your official pdsition as Chairman of the Local Board of Widnes. I would ask, first, is it fair or right, or rather I should ask, is it a rule of the Hospital that a medical man residing in another town. having an unqualified assistant living in Widnes is allowed the same locus standi, and equal opportunities of practice in the Widnes Accident Hospital as resident medical practitioners? Second, do you allow unqualified men to take the responsibilities of the hospital practice on their shoulders, and have they an equal footing there as local medical men? Rule third states definitely that each patient is to choose a duly qualified medical man, but I find that nnqualffied men are admitted and freely practice in hospital. Some unqualified assistants attend hospital under the immediate superintendence of their principals, and no man can reasonably object to that. There are many other matters requiring consideration ant rectification, about which the Hospital Committee, so far as I know, do not consult the medical men of Widnes. I also find that suggestions made by medical men—written in the practitioners' book and passed by the Board—are not carried into efftct. Consequently, I see no 6ther way of having such irregularities corrected than by applying to you, as chairman of the Local Board of Widnes, and ask you to be kind enough to bring up these matters for con- sideration before the local authority.—Yours truly, D. URIIITHIIRT MACLENNAN, M.B.(Edin.)' —Mr. HANDLEY : think that letrer might be referred to the Hospital Com- mittee, who could take it into consideration.—Dr. O'KEassa : Mr. Chairman, before that is done I think that I might say something upon the matter. The letter has been addressed to you, sir, as chairman of the Board, and not to the chairman of the Hospital Committee, if it had been addressed to the chairman of the last-named committee, it would, probably, not have been brought before us at all. The matter might, under those circumstances, ,have been allowed to rest in peace; but inasmuch as the communica- tion is addressed to you,.as chairman of the Board, I con- sider it is a matter for discussion by the members. As a medical man practising in Widnes I certainly sympathise with the remarks contained in that letter, believing, as I, do, that the rules of the hospital require amending. We ought not to allow unqualified practitioners to come to our hospital and attend cases there, unless, as Dr. MacLennan says, under the immediate superintendence of the men for whom they are working. I, as well as all the medical men in Widnes, am of opinion that no strangers—that is to say men who live out of the township and district of Widnes— should to allowed to attend patients in our hospital; and, if a rule permitting that practice exists, the sooner it is rescinded and the better. Is fact, I propose that if it be in existence, it be rescinded.—After some further discussion it was agreed, on the recOmmendation of the Chairman, that the communication be referred ba ak to the Hospital Com- mittee, and after they had reported upon it, it could be die- cussed.—Mr:HANDLEY considered 'that Dr. O'Keefifa had brought a very serious charge against the committee, which was a reflection upon them.—Dr. O'KEEFE was undastood to say that he did not intend to convey such a meaning by I the remarks he had made.—The CHAIRMAN : I think that you need not take any notice of, it Mr. Handley. div.head: PRICE OF GAS,
div.p: THE PRICE OF GAS,

" The minutes of the Gas and Water Committee were con- firmed, on the proposition of Mr. GA WELL, seconded by Mr. Buowtv.—Mr. GASKELL said he was glad ta see that the quality of the gas was muck better than it used to be. It was now 18 candles as against 16 formerly. They were also making the article cheaper, so that he hoped when they had entered into their new contracts at the end ef the finan- cial year, they would be able to recommend the Board to make a reduction in the price of gas. (Hear, hear.) The works were not insured at the present, and they were liable to an explosion similar to the one which occurred at Birken- head. They could insure them at an exceedingly favour- able rate, which would be a far better course than coming upon the ratepayers for £lB,OOO or £20,000 if a serious accident 'happened. He moved that the insurance be entered into.—Mr. KErtsuivir seconded the motion, which was passed.
