IMPORTANT MEETING OF RUNCORN FREEHOLDERS.

On Wednesday evening, a meeting of Runcorn freeholders, called by Dr. Steele, chairman of the Commissioners, was held in the Board-room, for the purpose of considering cer- tain illegal enclosures of the common land, which had been brought under the notice of that body. Mr. Philip Speak- man was voted to the chair, and there were also present Messrs-. T. Normam, Robert Shaw, Joseph Williams, James Kirkham, Samuel White, Thomas Booth, William Leach, William Guest, Samuel Yarwood, J. J. Speakman, Thomas Berry (Bridgewater and Ellesmere Trustees), Thomas Hand- ley, James Wilson, F. Fairhurst, William Handley, W. Sutton, E. Irnison, Edward Taylor, and R. Forrester.—The Chairman read the notice convening the meeting, and called upon Mr. Brookes (secretary to the Commissioners) to read the minutes which had been passed at the meetings of the Board in relation to the Freeholders' Rights Committee; and the report of Mr. Barker,. surveyor, ore the subject.— Mr. Brookes, having read these documents, copies of which have already appeared in the Examiner, the Chairman re- marked that they had to consider that night, wasewhat action they, as freeholders, should take as to the alleged encroach- ments. To his mind, it would boa very serious matter to pull any fence down, unless they knew their exact legal posi- tion on the question. They had, perhaps, better consider whether they should not move on the lines laid down by the Act of Parliament. If they resolved themselves into a committee to exercise their powers under the Enclosure Acts, then all who had encroached on the rights of the free- holders could be proceeded against in a proper legal form. He simply threw out these ideas in order to put the matter before them into some kind of form for discussion.---Mr. William Handley: Has Mr. Frodsham been communicated with, on behalf of the Freeholders' Committee 11—Mr. Brookes : Yes, sir.—Mr. Handley: And what reply has he sent P—Mr. Barker : No reply at all, sir.—Mr. Shaw said he understood that Mr. Frodsham sent an answer to the effect that he had received permission to do what he had done from the Marquis of Cholmondley.—The Chairman observed that the comrnit ee had been informed by Mr. Beswiek, agent to the Marquis, that he was not aware of any agree- ment between his employer and Mr. Jno..Frodsharn, as to the enclosure of any land. The Chairman wished to state that the cost of any action they might take would have to come out of the pockets of the freeholders, are it could not be paid out of the rates.—Mr. T. Booth: Would it benefit the tree- holders if these spots were laid waste again ?—The Chair- man: That is not exactly the question, which is whether one person has any right more than another to enclose any piece of land.—ln answer to a question, Mr. Norman said the rights of the Marquis applied to all minerals, but the freeholders had to do with the surface.—Mr. Shaw, observed that what was everybody's business was nobody's business ;-and it was highly probable that instead of decreasing, the number of enclosures in the future would increase. They might get powers so that the whole of the common land could be en- closed, or they might bring the question in dispute before the judge of the county court, when those who had enclosed land would have to make good their title to it.—Mr. William Handley remarked that if one third in value of-the free- holders passed a resolution vesting the matter in the Com- missioners, that body could take the question up. He agreed with Mr. Shaw that it would be better to consider the broad question at issue, rather than to deal with narrow issues. As the stone was taken out of the land, it would be possible to 4 secure the latter as a breathing lung for Runcorn for all time. He believed that the Marquis of Cholmondley, in consenting to stone being taken from the hill by Mr. Guest, had agreed that the land should be levelled, so as to be tit for the. use of the town af lel-wards. 'They ought certainly to take some steps for keeping sacred Beacon Hill as a land-mark in the history of Runcorn. That bill was one of the early land- marks which pointed out a period in the history of the country when telegraph poles were unknown, and when the beacon fires were lighted upon it, in the case of incursions from the Danes up the Mersey, the alarm was given to the people on the Welsh hills and to the population living with- in the wide sweep of twelve or thirteen English counties. Perhaps Mr. Berry was in a position to make some state- ment on behalf of the Bridgewater and Ellesmere truetees.--- Mr. nervy replied that Imeould scarcely do this, as he merely attended the meeting to report the course whish the free- holders proposed to adopt.—The Secretary read a clause from the Act of Parliament showing that any urban sani- tary authority might, with the ce,nsent of persons repeesent- ing, at least one-third in value of the interest in any subur- ban common, make an application to the Enclosure Commis- sioners for the regulation of snob commore—On the motion of Mr. Norman, seconded by Mr. Williams, the following gentlemen were appointed a committee to take the whole matter into coeeideration e—Messrs. J Speakman, Robert Shaw, ThotnaA Norman, W. Handley, R. Fmrester, S. C. Beckett, Sarnuel White, James Wilson, J. J. Speakman, W. Leach, and James Kirkham.—On the proposition of Mr. Shaw, seconded by Mr. Williams, it resolved that the requisite steps should be taken to secure the conseat of at least on third of the fteeholders to the action pre,p(A«l to be taken.—Mr. Norman, moved, an Mr. Forrester, seconded the appointment of Mr. William Handley as secretary, whir' was carried nneninsously aftee which, the, ttrahatecl,

•DISTRICT OF RUNCORN. • THE PUBLIQ LIBRARIES' ACTS, 1855-1866-1871-1877. [Received December 6th. 1881.1 To the Chairman and Memeers of the Board et Improvement Commissioners for the 'Astrid of Runcorn. Whereas by an Act of Parliament passed in the /Bth and 19th years of Queen Victoria. chapter 70, entitnled "The Public Libraries' Act, 1855, which Act was amended by another Act, passed in the 29111 and 30th years of the reign of Queen Victoria, chapter 114. intituled "The Public libraries' Amendment Act, 1866," it is provided that "The Board of any District being a place within the limits of any Improvement Aet, shall up in the Requisition in Writing of at least ten persons assessed to, and paying the General District Rate, appoint a time not less than ten days nor more than twenty days from the time of receiving suck Requisition for a Public Meeting of the persons assessed to, and paying such rate, in order to determine whether these Acts shall be adopted for such Districts, we, the undersigned, being persons assessed to, and paying Rates to the Improvement Commissioners for the District of Runcorn, do hereby respect- fully request you to call a Meeting of persons assessed to and paying Rates to your Board, for the purpose of determining whether or not the above mentioned Acts shall be adopted for such Districts, in manner provided by the said Acts. We are, Sir and Gentlemen, yours respectfully, Finlay MoDougall, William Handley, Henry Randle, H. Sefton, J. 0. Jackson, Alfred Buck, Willlatn Preston, MA., Richard Lea, Wiliam Haainson, John Buckley, Thomas H. Annett, Joseph Pollitt, Francis Fairhurst, George Bellamy, W. IL Rogerson, Henry Briscoe, Henry Johnson, Ashes Uns worth, James B. Bankes, James MeQuinn, James Craig, George Marshall, Samuel 0, Beckett, George Summerfteld, W. J. Shore, Thomas Harris' William B..te, Ralph Forrester, John W. Lightburn, Samuel Crosby, George Rhodes, John Simpson, Joseph H. Diggles. In accordance with the above Requisition, I hereby convene a PUBLIC MEETING of the porton.; assessed to, and paying the General District Rate, for the District of Runcorm to be held in BATEIESDA SCROOL-ROO3l, VICAR-STREET, Rusiccraw, at Seven o'clock in the Evening, on ktaanAv, the 19th day of DECEMBRR, 1381. MAT. STEELE, Chairman of the Runcorn Improvement Commissioners.
